stories.body:
Beijing warns against ‘discriminatory’ step after France drops opposition to British role in Made in Europe package

No 10 has left the door open to imposing tariffs on Chinese-made electric vehicles as part of the Made in Europe package, prompting a warning from Beijing that such a move would be “discriminatory”.

Downing Street said on Friday that it would “welcome the objective to have the UK included in the Industrial Accelerator Act” after France dropped its opposition to Britain joining the scheme .

The aim of the rules is to curb subsidised Chinese imports by giving EU-made products preferential treatment, but the UK and others such as Norway are worried about being left at a disadvantage if excluded from the scheme.

The price for joining would be aligning with the EU’s tariffs on Chinese EVs imposed by the bloc in 2024, according to a Franco-German proposal on Thursday night that said the UK would have to dynamically align with EU trade defence measures.

The Chinese embassy in London said it was “firmly opposed to any discriminatory practice involving tariff hikes or restrictive measures on Chinese products”. “We have expressed serious concern to the UK side regarding the reports in question,” it said, adding that “trade protectionism runs counter to WTO rules and market principles”.

This week, the business secretary, Jonathan Reynolds, said he would not be coerced into aligning with the EU’s policy.

However, the government has been desperate to be included in the Made in Europe package, fearing billions of pounds of trade in the car industry could be lost if the UK is locked out of supply chains in the EU.

Asked whether the UK accepted it would have to put tariffs on Chinese-made vehicles in order to join Made in Europe, a No 10 spokesperson said it was “premature to speculate” on the terms of any deal with the bloc and there was “still a European process to run”.

They added: “But more broadly, on the principle, the UK obviously has its own trade policy and it keeps all tariffs under review. And we work closely with the British automotive sector to make sure that that approach reflects their best interests.”

Chinese EVs are increasingly popular, with BYD sales up 78% year on year in September, Chery up 660% and the lesser-known Changan up by more than 3,000% in terms of market share.

EU lawmakers are expected to finalise the Industrial Accelerator Act, known as Made in Europe legislation, by the end of the year or early 2027.

But MEPs have already tabled 5,100 amendments, including one embracing the UK and giving Andy Burnham time to secure the deal he wants.

Earlier this week the boss of Mercedes-Benz, Ola Källenius, who is also the president of the European car trade body ACEA, warned that locking the UK out of legislation would amount to a “deliberate choice” by EU leaders to “hurt” the car industry across the bloc.

According to the new Franco-German proposal, there would be “an opt-in to further include European partners who were part of the EU single market as of 1 January 2020”, which includes the UK and Norway.

This would be provided those third countries accepted “dynamic alignment on the EU’s conditions related to third countries’ investments and on relevant EU trade defence measures”.

Tariffs could help UK-based manufacturers by preventing cut-price Chinese models flooding the market but they could also push up prices for consumers and harm British manufacturers trying to sell vehicles to China in the case of an escalating trade war. About 80% of UK-made cars are exported, with more than half going to the EU and 6% to China.

Earlier on Thursday the trade minister, Anas Sarwar, hinted that the UK was minded to align on tariffs. He told Politico the UK and the EU must “work together and act in lockstep” to tackle China’s dominance in the automotive sector.

A car industry source said the EU “has recently shown that it is possible to have a dialogue with the Chinese and get some form of safeguarding in place” without retaliation.

China opposes the expansion of EV tariffs. In the past few months it has made what European Commission officials called “bloodcurdling threats” to launch a trade war over the latest plan to impose quotas on Chinese hybrid cars.

While quotas can be introduced within months under World Trade Organization rules, it could take more than a year to impose tariffs on Chinese cars, with strict processes to be followed, starting with notification of an investigation and followed by evidence-gathering and sharing over alleged harms China might be causing to the British car industry.

Liam Byrne, the Labour chair of the parliamentary business committee, has said imposing tariffs on Chinese EVs would be “a small price to pay” to save the industry in both the UK and the EU.

At a conference in London on Thursday night, he said the UK “urgently needs” a new strategy on China to ensure that British and European manufacturing “does not die”.

Byrne, who has been leading an investigation into the UK’s position on China, was highly critical of the government’s approach, which he believes is naive and based on false hopes that China will change its export policy.

“Our China strategy is simply not where it needs to be. The UK urgently needs a coherent China strategy, which it does not have today,” he said.

stories.body:
Supporters of planned tax, however, say banks were bailed out by taxpayers during financial crisis and can afford to pay more now

John Healey poised to raise taxes on banks in budget

The International Monetary Fund has urged John Healey to target savings on pensions and welfare, instead of taxing Britain’s banks at the budget later this month.

Helge Berger, deputy director of the IMF’s European department, was asked about bank taxes after the Guardian revealed Healey plans to tap the sector for additional revenue.

Berger replied that given the UK’s current high tax-to-GDP ratio, it might be better to “put the emphasis” on cuts.

He said if additional tax revenue were needed, reforming property taxes or VAT might be a good place to start.

He added: “Ultimately, with taxes roughly at 40% of GDP – historically, for Britain, a high number – then of course balancing these measures on the fiscal [spending] side, doing a bit more there, makes good sense.”

As examples, he highlighted the pensions triple lock – which Labour has already said it will reform – and “better targeting [of] social benefits”, adding: “I think that’s where you would put the emphasis, rather than the tax that you mentioned.”

Berger was speaking in Bangkok, where the IMF has held its annual meetings this week.

City lobbyists have been out in full force, warning the government that higher taxes could force banks to throttle lending, hitting the economy and even forcing some lenders to move jobs and operations abroad.

In a letter sent to Healey and copied to the prime minister, Andy Burnham, on 12 October, days before news of the planned tax hike broke, the chief executive of UK Finance, David Postings, shared research commissioned by the lobby group.

It suggested that reversing Tory cuts to the bank surcharge – taking it back to 8% from 3% – would leave annual UK GDP £1.2bn lower in real terms by 2029-30 than it would have otherwise been.

He said it would also see banks issue fewer business loans and mortgages, with lending likely to be £10.4bn lower in 2029-2030 than if the surcharge was held at 3%.

“The UK’s banking sector already makes a vital contribution to the wider economy,” Postings’ letter said. “To sustain this vital contribution, the budget should avoid any increases in bank-specific taxes, as this would risk constraining the sector’s ability to lend and invest.”

However, TUC analysis of HMRC corporate tax receipts shows the Treasury has already lost out on £6bn over the three years since the surcharge cut came into force in 2023.

At the same time, banks have been reporting strong profits, largely off the back of high interest rates, with bosses subsequently increasing banker bonus pots and handing billions of pounds to shareholders.

Collectively, the UK’s four largest lenders – HSBC, NatWest, Barclays and Lloyds – reported £29.2bn in profits over the first six months of the year, with almost half, £13.7bn, pledged to investors through dividends and share buybacks. Over the past five years, those banks have raked in £200bn in pre-tax profits.

after newsletter promotion

Author and former banker Philip Augar said the banks were “enjoying boom conditions”, partly due to good management but partly due to economic conditions “not of their own making”. He said there was room for a “moderate increase in taxation” that would raise about £2bn to £3bn a year.

“The prime minister has said that the burden of taxation has to fall on those with the broader shoulders, and at the moment, it’s hard to think of a sector where the shoulders are much broader than the banking sector,” Augar told the BBC’s Today programme on Friday.

While banks could not expect interest rates benefits to continue forever, Augar said that banks – including those that were bailed out in the 2008 financial crisis – could not have it both ways.

“Banking is cyclical, it’s true. But when it hits really rocky times it expects the taxpayer to bail them out,” Augar said. “When it hits boom times, it expects some kind of special treatment. Banks can’t be too big to fail and too big to tax.”

Some banks have threatened to pull investment, and potentially jobs, from the UK if it hikes taxes, with lobby groups noting smaller overall tax charges in rival financial centres like Frankfurt, Dublin and Amsterdam.

Jamie Dimon, who heads up the largest bank in the US, JP Morgan, said in May that he could scrap plans for a new £3bn London headquarters if the UK government became hostile towards banks.

But Augar said the government needed to see past the bluster. “There seems to have been a coordinated campaign by the big international banks who have businesses in Britain – JP Morgan, Citigroup, Santander, HSBC and others.

“But they always say this, [and] they rarely move. I think that if the chancellor judges this right, with a moderate increase in taxation or some other form of getting money from the banks, then the business will remain in the UK.”

stories.body:
How architects worked with harsh environment to create sustainable building in location where fossils were found

V iewed from afar, the silver-hued Hami Pterosaur Museum almost looks like a space base on Mars. Viewed from above, it resembles a collection of dinosaur eggs in the sand. Nestled in the Gobi desert, in north-west China , the new tourist attraction showcases hundreds of impressive fossils of pterosaurs, ancient flying reptiles related to dinosaurs. But far from reflecting its prehistoric exhibits, the building itself is a modern-day architectural specimen.

Designed with underground exhibition halls, giant light funnels and sprawling solar farms, the museum is able to operate sustainably while withstanding an extremely harsh environment.

The Hami region is notorious for its scorching summers. Air temperatures can exceed 55C (131F), while the surface ground temperature can reach 80C, says Wang Xiaolin, the director of the museum and a palaeontologist at the Chinese Academy of Sciences. Violent winds and sandstorms terrorise the area frequently, according to Xiaolin, who has carried out excavation work in Hami for 20 years.

Despite the intimidating conditions, building the museum in the area is important from a scientific perspective because this is where the fossils were buried and found, Xiaolin says. Keeping the fossils local protects the fragile relics and lets visitors see them in their geological context, he adds.

Visitors to the five exhibition halls can expect to see precious fossils discovered by Xiaolin’s team, including one that has preserved the upper and lower jaws, as well as the soft-tissue structures of the head crest of a pterosaur that roamed the area roughly 130m years ago.

Most of the 8,000-sq metre museum is built 8 metres into the ground where temperatures are much lower, which helps it stay cool in summer, says Huai Kaifeng, an architect at Beijing-based Turenscape, which designed the project. In winter, when temperatures can drop below -20C, the design also helps the museum stay warm.

Being largely underground, with seven above-ground entrances, allows the museum to use its energy as efficiently as possible, says Wang Yujia, a landscape architect and associate professor at the University of Nebraska–Lincoln in the US, who is not involved in the project. Most of it is able to avoid direct exposure to wind, sand and solar heat and the large temperature swings between day and night in the desert. “This all means that you need much, much less air-conditioning,” Yujia says.

Although air-conditioners have been installed to provide backup, the museum has natural ventilation shafts that allow cool air to sink and hot air to rise and escape. The museum can cut its electricity usage on air conditioning by 94% compared with an above-ground counterpart, according to estimates by Turenscape. This equates to a saving of 223,421kWh of electricity annually – enough to power an average UK home for 89 years.

But the underground space in the desert presented another challenge for the architects: lighting. The team used giant, translucent, ceiling-to-floor funnels to let in as much natural light as possible. These structures slash the museum’s need for artificial lighting by nearly 50%, saving 84,672kWh of electricity a year, according to Turenscape.

The museum was one of the last designs completed by the late Chinese landscape architect Kongjian Yu , the founder of Turenscape. Yu was the brain behind China’s “ sponge cities ”, a concept that uses nature to prevent flooding in urban areas.

after newsletter promotion

The museum has its own micro power grid, featuring a solar farm and batteries to store energy. The solar farm is about 1km from the museum, with an outline resembling that of a pterosaur when viewed from above. It is expected to generate more than 22.4GWh of electricity a year, enough to meet the museum’s own demand, Huai says. The museum is still connected to the power grid of the nearby city of Hami to ensure its energy security, he notes.

The museum is also connected to Hami’s water-supplying network, but it has a recycling system on site to collect, process and reuse its grey water.

“Water is precious out here in the Gobi,” Xiaolin says.

For Yujia, the museum is a good example of how a building can be designed to adapt to its natural environment rather than fight against it.

Although technology enables people to build luxury resorts in a desert and keep them cool, such projects require huge amounts of energy and resources, he says.

“It makes sense to work as much as possible with the environmental conditions that are already there, instead of relying entirely on technology to isolate the building from them.”

Examples include a floating exhibition pavilion built in Rotterdam to address rising sea levels, and a giant park with a tilted ground in Bangkok that aims to prevent urban flooding, and a home shaped like a snail’s shell in Iran to help its inhabitants stay cool.

The concept is important for arid areas. “These places are not cities, you don’t necessarily have the basic infrastructure or the resources you desire even if you pay, because money is not magic,” Yujia adds.

Designing buildings and parks to combat natural disasters was a lasting theme throughout Yu’s career, and for Jiinyi Hwang, the chief architect at Turenscape, the museum is no exception.

“Our world is drying. Deserts and arid zones are expanding. Cities are warming. More and more of the built environment is being pushed into climates that were once considered unbuildable,” Hwang says. “If we keep designing with the same assumptions – sealed boxes, glass facades and mechanical climate control – we will consume the very resources these landscapes cannot spare.”

stories.body:
Shevaun Haviland argues PM is right to revisit Labour’s EU red lines as current trading relationship is bad for business

Repairing the economic damage of Brexit should be the top priority for Andy Burnham as he reconsiders Labour’s red lines on EU membership, the head of one of Britain’s leading business groups has said.

Shevaun Haviland, the director general of the British Chambers of Commerce (BCC), said she welcomed the prime minister reopening the Brexit battle lines despite the uncertainty it could create, arguing that the UK’s current trading relationship with the EU was bad for business.

“We do think it’s right, because of what we know from the evidence of how businesses feel it’s not working,” she said.

Highlighting the continuing economic hit from Brexit , Haviland said more than half of bosses surveyed by the business lobby group believed the deal negotiated by Boris Johnson’s government and enacted in 2021 was not helping them.

“We expected it to be very difficult at the beginning, when [companies] were getting used to the new rules, and then it would sort of get easier as it went to along. But actually, that has not happened,” she said.

Economists estimate the cost to the UK economy has been up to £240bn so far , with national income per head between 6% and 8% lower than it would have been had the UK not left the EU. The Office for Budget Responsibility estimates a long-term hit of about 4% of gross domestic product.

At Labour’s conference in Liverpool last month, Burnham said Brexit had done “more harm than good” as he pledged to reassess Britain’s relationship with the EU. He opened the door to options including fully rejoining the bloc, and this week he said failing to pursue a better deal with the EU would be a “major dereliction of duty” .

In an interview with the Guardian in Norwich alongside the head of the Norfolk Chambers of Commerce (NCC) chief executive, Nova Fairbanks, Haviland said the government had to take into account business frustrations with Brexit .

She said the BCC would also consult its 50,000 members, who collectively employ more than 6 million people across the UK, on a range of options for Britain’s relationship, including rejoining the EU.

“We are 10 years since the referendum,” Haviland said. “We would say the language of Brexit needs to move on. That’s gone. What businesses understand is what we had before and what we’ve got now.

“We’re apolitical, it’s not a political question. It is an economic question. So we are going to set out the options, from the where we are to the most extreme. And in consultation with our chambers, and our partners, we will see where people are.”

Fairbanks said it was clear that some Brexit-backing bosses recognised the economic damage. “It would be very interesting to see how many businesses that were very much pro-Brexit are still pro-Brexit, because I’ve certainly not heard any change of heart from those that were against Brexit. I think they are still very much: ‘We need to be closer to Europe.’”

after newsletter promotion

Speaking on the sidelines of an NCC trade fair at the Norfolk Showground, the business leaders said companies were coming under growing pressure from rising energy prices and other effects of the war in the Middle East.

Haviland called on the chancellor, John Healey, to take bold action at this month’s budget to support firms despite concerns at the heart of government about the pressure on the public finances amid jitters in the bond market .

“This rumour about a sort of ‘steady as she goes’ budget, and ‘let’s not upset the apple cart’. Business don’t really want just a ‘steady as she goes’. They want to see some action that will relieve some of those costs that will drive that fly wheel [of the British economy],” she said.

“You can’t just trot along in a crouch position effectively. And surely the markets will be happy to see some spending cuts by the government, and some investment in private-sector growth?”

Haviland called for action on energy bills, business rates and taxes on employment to help companies recruit more young people. “In your energy bill, about 40% of your energy is actually energy. The other 60% is about tax. So the government can get some of that out,” she said.

“The big test for the chancellor is to put his money where his mouth is for business at the budget. Just showing that he genuinely believes that the wealth creators are the job creators – which is business.”

stories.body:
Healey quizzed about bank tax plans

Over at the IMF’s annual meeting in Bangkok today, chancellor John Healey is meeting with UK journalists now, including my colleague Heather Stewart .

Healey , who should be cheered by the news that the UK economy grew unexpectedly in August , was asked whether he plans to impose new taxes on the bank sector, and replies:

double quotation mark “I don’t want anybody to try and read in or second guess what [we may] do in two weeks’ time. My observations on the banks are just that people too often see them as a big distant financial institutions, when they are hardwired into the economic fabric of this country and our future prospects. That said, you know I’ve got decisions to take in the in the budget, and I will. I’ll set those out in two weeks’ time.

Healey added that his “special responsibility as Chancellor is to protect the resilience of the British economy for the future” – echoing what he told Sky News a few minutes ago .

The chancellor also welcomed the IMF’s support for the UK’s fiscal plans.

Closing post

Time to wrap up.

The US inflation squeeze has intensified, with new data showing that US producer prices rose in September at the fastest pace in more than four years.

With higher energy costs hitting the US economy, the producer price index advanced 1.3% from a month earlier — the most since March 2022. On an annual basis, prices were 6.3% higher.

The data helped to push down shares on Wall Street, as an accelerating sell-off of AI-linked shares has hit global markets.

South Korea’s benchmark Kospi 200 index, which is heavily skewed towards the companies that make memory chips, fell more than 8% overnight to a six-month closing low, triggering circuit breakers that brought trading to a halt at various points.

Some of those semiconductor stocks, such as SK Hynix and Samsung Electronics, plunged nearly 11% and 9.5% respectively. The index closed at a six-month low, down 8.1%.

US stocks fell further when trading resumed on Thursday. The Nasdaq dropped another 1.4% at the start of trading, with Dell , which makes datacentre servers, and Coherent , which manufactures components for AI datacentres, leading the early fallers.

The UK rallied, though, helped by the news that Britain’s economy kept growing.

Figures from the Office for National Statistics showed gross domestic product (GDP) rose by 0.1% last month, compared with 0.4% growth in July. That confounded a forecast by City economists of a 0.1% contraction.

With less than a fortnight before the budget, the ONS reading represents a surprise boost given that the Middle East war is rattling the global economy and hitting British households and businesses with a surge in energy costs.

John Healey has promised to use his first budget in a fortnight’s time to offer consumers and businesses a “breathing space” while sticking to Labour’s fiscal rules.

Speaking to journalists in Bangkok, where he has been attending the International Monetary Fund annual meetings, the chancellor said he was conscious of rising costs.

Healey also hailed the contribution that UK banks make, calling them part of the ‘jewel in the crown’ – amid speculation that he could impose higher taxes on them in the budget.

He told reporters:

double quotation mark My observations on the banks are just that people too often see them as a big distant financial institutions, when they are hardwired into the economic fabric of this country and our future prospects.

Some Labour MPs want the chancellor to raise taxes on the gambling sector .

US lawmakers unveil bill to hold Wall Street’s ‘Epstein-connected’ bosses to account

US lawmakers have unveiled a new bill to hold Wall Street’s “Epstein-connected” bosses to account for helping finance the late sex offender’s crimes.

It came as top Democratic senator Elizabeth Warren condemned the UK bank Barclays for “dodging responsibility” over its failure to vet former boss Jes Staley and his ties to the once well-connected billionaire.

A bipartisan group of politicians, led by Warren and House representative Robert Garcia, are introducing a bill on Thursday known as the Epstein Wall Street Records Act. The bill follows a months-long investigation into the financier, who died in prison in 2019 while awaiting trial on child sex-trafficking charges.

If passed, the bill would force regulators including the Federal Reserve and the Securities and Exchange Commission to investigate “Epstein connected” financial firms and executives for potential breaches of banking, investment or illicit funding laws; and fine or even ban wrongdoers from the US financial sector.

FTSE 100 hits five-week high

The UK stock market is continuing to benefit from turmoil elsewhere.

The FTSE 100 share index is now up 1.1% at 10,843 points, its highest level since 8 September.

Kathleen Brooks, research director at XTB, says US assets are acting like a ‘harbour in the storm’:

double quotation mark A stronger economy, combined with a resilient FTSE 100, which is the best performing major index so far this week, is good news for the pound and the Gilt market. As other markets crash and burn, the pound is the top performing G7 currency this week, and the Gilt market is the best performer amongst its peers on Thursday. When the AI trade sells off, the UK is the harbour in the storm.

The US economy is continuing to hold onto workers, despite inflationary pressures.

The number of Americans filing new claims for unemployment support remained low last week, at 199,000 - 1,000 more than a week earlier.

Coherent Corp , the US manufacturer of lasers, engineered materials, and optoelectronic components for AI data centres, is also caught up in the sell-off – its shares are down 9%.

Europe has to take action to curb soaring oil and gas prices to prevent people from turning to populists and extremists, a senior EU official has said.

Dan Jørgensen, the European commissioner for energy and housing policy, said EU governments could choose actions to make fossil fuels cheaper as long as they were “targeted” and “temporary” so as not to derail the continent from its goal to tackle the climate crisis by drastically cutting carbon emissions.

Our Europe Live blog has all the details:

Dell (-9%) are leading the fallers on the S&P 500, as doubts persist about the AI boom.

That adds to their 11% drop yesterday, after analysts at Barclays raised concerns that enterprise spending on artificial intelligence won’t justify the AI buildout.

Wall Street opens in the red

Stocks are dropping on Wall Street at the start of trading, as inflation worries and AI angst hit share prices.

Tech stocks are leading the sell-off, pulling the Nasdaq index down by 1.3%.

The broader S&P 500 share index has dropped by 0.5%.

This morning’s jump in the US PPI index will have raised concerns about inflationary pressures.

Traders are also reacting to the sell-off in Asia-Pacific markets overnight, where South Korea’s Kospi hit a six-month low overnight ( see earlier post ).

On the AI front, AstraZeneca has entered into a new collaboration with a Californian AI therapeuticscompany called insitro , aimed at identifying novel targets to develop medicines for liver and heart disease.

The collaboration will focus on the areas of metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis (MASH), a serious liver disease, and cardiomyopathies, diseases of the heart muscle.

Insitro has created a virtual human to generate large-scale human and cellular data with AI-enabled target identification and medicine design. The deal is worth $1.46bn, with $40m paid upfront by AstraZeneca . The Californian company also has partnerships with US drugmakers Bristol Myers-Squibb and Eli Lilly.

Sharon Barr , executive vice resident and head of biopharmaceuticals research & development at AstraZeneca , said:

double quotation mark “We know that disease biology is incredibly complex, and one of the most critical decisions in R&D is selecting the right target. This strategic collaboration underscores our commitment to maximising the potential of cutting-edge AI to tackle the root cause of disease. Partnering with insitro, we will use advanced AI to identify the biological drivers of disease to support the rapid discovery of high-quality novel targets, advancing our ambition to deliver the next generation of medicines to patients faster.”

Today’s jump in wholesale US inflation increases the pressure on the US Federal Reserve to raise interest rates soon.

Waleed Said , technical analyst at GivTrade , says the increase in core PPI means the energy shock from the Iran war is spreading, adding:

double quotation mark A firmer Fed is more likely but the market pricing about a one in three chance of a hike in October so don’t overreact to the headline but a rate hike in December does seem imminent.

US PPI inflation driven up by soaring gasoline

Tin hats on!

New data from the US has shown that producers are hiking prices at their fastest rate in almost four years, and much faster than expected.

Ths increase was driven by a surge in energy prices, which more than wiped out a drop in egg prices.

The Producer Price Index, which measures how much goods makers and services firms charge for their wares, jumped by 6.3% in the year to September. That’s the largest 12-month increase since December 2022, when it rose by 6.4%.

On a monthly basis, prices climbed by 1.2% in September alone, a sign that inflationary pressures rose last month.

The report shows that goods prices jumped by 2.6% in September alone, the largest increase since data were first calculated in December 2009.

That was driven by the rise in motor fuel; The Bureau of Labor Statistics reports:

double quotation mark Half of the September increase in the index for final demand goods can be traced to prices for gasoline, which jumped 20.3 percent. The indexes for diesel fuel, fresh and dry vegetables, jet fuel, residential electric power, and crude petroleum also rose. In contrast, prices for chicken eggs dropped 39.7 percent.

Alarmingly, core PPI also jumped. Prices for final demand less foods, energy, and trade services rose 5.0% in the year to September.

PPI is an important measure, as increases in producer prices tend to be passed onto consumers, who already experienced a jump in inflation last month:

EU pushing for action over trade deficit with China

The EU is set to call for further action to curb the bloc’s vast trade deficit with China, widely blamed for job losses and factory closures across the continent.

EU leaders meeting in Brussels on Thursday to discuss the trade deficit with China - which hit €360bn in 2025 - are expected to call for “new instruments to better address these imbalances” according to a draft statement.

The European Commission, which negotiates trade policy on behalf of the 27 member states, agreed a deal this month with Beijing that will see the EU limit hybrid car exports from China to 350,000 vehicles a year, potentially halving Chinese market share.

EU countries have welcomed the deal, but think it is not enough and want steps to protect other industrial sectors, such as chemicals, plastics and machinery.

The debate has sharpened since Germany - long reluctant to use trade defences against China - converted to a more hawkish position amid pressure from German industrial leaders, who are laying off workers and closing factories.

Germany and France last week called for better use of existing trade defence measures, including urgent action in the chemicals and plastics sectors.

The EU’s two biggest economies are also seeking “a diversification instrument” that would cut off access to the EU market when faced with severe imbalances. Dubbed the “kill switch”, the law is intended to be country agnostic, but is clearly aimed at China.

Member states have welcomed the deal negotiated by EU trade commissioner Maroš Šefčovič on hybrid cars, but are sceptical as to whether Beijing will stick to it. China would adhere to the agreement because they began to realise “they are killing their customers” , Šefčovič was reported to have said, according to a senior EU diplomat.

The EU diplomat highlighted the urgency of the situation from the EU’s point of view: “We don’t have much time because every month that goes by, thousands of jobs are lost.”

UK government says it is minded to intervene in Sky-ITV deal

Media news: The UK government is ‘minded to intervene’ in Sky’s£1.6bn deal to buy ITV’s broadcasting and streaming arm.

Lisa Nandy, secretary of state for Digital, Culture, Media and Sport, has told parliament she believes there are public interest grounds for intervening in the deal.

They include ‘the need for free expression of opinion in news media’, the need for a pluratity of views in the news, and the need for a wide range of broadcasting which is “of high quality and calculated to appeal to a wide variety of tastes and interests.”

Back in July, Sky said the deal was a chance to create a “UK-focused national streaming champion”.

stories.summary: Sky-high oil prices and geopolitical turmoil have made less of a dent than feared … just don’t bank on it to last Inside the vast, glass-walled Queen Sirikit conference centre in Bangkok, the air-conditioned atmosphere was calm as policymakers from more than 100 countries gathered this week for the International Monetary Fund’s annual meeting – and contemplated the surprising strength of the global economy. stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Sky-high oil prices and geopolitical turmoil have made less of a dent than feared … just don’t bank on it to last

I nside the vast, glass-walled Queen Sirikit conference centre in Bangkok, the air-conditioned atmosphere was calm as policymakers from more than 100 countries gathered this week for the International Monetary Fund’s annual meeting – and contemplated the surprising strength of the global economy.

A small army of smiling, uniformed Thai staff were on hand to explain the baffling geography of the heavily guarded building, where lunch options were as cosmopolitan as the delegates – including, improbably, a Burger King.

“Resilience” was the buzzword at one event after another, after six months in which sky-high oil prices and geopolitical chaos have made less of a dent in the global economy than first feared.

Growth has not fallen off a cliff, buoyed up by the AI investment boom; stock markets haven’t crashed. “We had Covid, the war in Ukraine, supply-chain shocks, the war in Iran, and the alarm bells go off. And yet we haven’t had that massive synchronised crisis. So I think there’s this feeling that a lot of countries are sort of defying gravity at all income levels,” said Clemence Landers, the vice-president of the Washington-based Center for Global Development.

Yet the IMF was also keen to remind delegates that the resilience of the past six months had been bought at a cost and may not last. The message – “Resilience under strain, urgent choices” – leapt out from the front page of its flagship publication, the World Economic Outlook (WEO).

According to IMF experts, the cost of the energy support measures governments have put in place to protect their citizens from soaring oil prices, as a result of Donald Trump’s war in Iran, has been an extraordinary 0.5% of global GDP.

It said many countries would be unable to sustain support on this scale for much longer – and some had already begun to phase out subsidies, exposing the public to more of the costs of the conflict.

The IMF urged governments to limit the costs and let market signals do their work, by sticking to temporary, targeted measures, rather than across-the-board subsidies.

Aside from how to cope with the practicalities of a conflict that has persisted far longer than many governments had hoped – and whose end point remains elusive – the IMF was also keen to highlight two pressing risks.

The first was what it sees as the unsustainable state of the public finances, particularly in the world’s richest countries. The WEO projected the highest budget deficits this year for advanced economies since the depths of the Covid pandemic.

That means government debt in these countries is expected to keep rising – from 108% of GDP last year, to 115% of GDP in five years’ time.

“Public debt is high in many economies, and fiscal buffers that could otherwise have helped meet rising spending pressures from ageing populations, climate change and national security needs have instead been used to absorb the repeated shocks,” the WEO said.

Anxiety about spendthrift governments appears to have been one factor driving the recent sell-off of government bonds – pushing up yields, or interest rates, to their highest levels in decades; though it also reflects higher expectations for inflation and growth.

The IMF’s managing director, Kristalina Georgieva , lamented: “Too many countries, they did not use the post-pandemic recovery to rebuild fiscal buffers, and each new shock has pushed debt levels higher.”

Fretting that this leaves governments exposed when the next shock comes, as well as pushing up the share of tax revenues required just to service debt, Georgieva repeatedly implored governments – not least Washington – to tighten their belts. “What is our loudest call to policymakers right now? Make urgent repairs to the fiscal house before the cracks widen,” she said. It seems a message unlikely to land well with voters buffeted by one shock after another.

The US Treasury secretary, Scott Bessent, did not bother to travel to Bangkok to hear it; nor to oversee the meeting of G20 finance ministers, of whom he is formally the chair this year.

The UK chancellor, John Healey, stepped in to chair the meeting instead. He spent much of his brief time in Bangkok stressing the importance of standing shoulder to shoulder with Ukraine – which the US has notably not been doing of late. Russia’s delegation was allowed to attend the G20 meeting, to the deep discomfort of UK delegates.

The UK received a positive review from Georgieva and her colleagues, for setting out a plan to balance the books; though she conceded the bond markets had not rewarded its prudence.

“The UK is actually one country where action to reduce the deficit has been taken decisively,” she said. Asked why the UK’s bond yields have not fallen accordingly, Georgieva said London’s status as a global financial centre tended to put the UK under additional scrutiny.

“Traditionally we’ve seen more attention, in relative terms in the UK, to what the government is doing. [There is] a bit more sensitivity, and I think the government recognises they need to stay the course.”

Unusually, no communique was issued after the G20 meeting: a stark signal of how difficult it has become to reach multilateral agreement in the current fissiparous period.

The UK will take over the G20 presidency next year and has ambitious plans, on AI regulation and international development; but Bessent’s no-show was a reminder of the tough task they face in rekindling multilateralism.

The other alarming message the IMF was keen to land, concerned the threat of an AI market crash. As Georgieva put it in a blogpost on Friday: “The risk is that expectations may run rapidly ahead of productivity gains, setting the stage for near-term disappointment.”

The Federal Reserve chair, Kevin Warsh, while professing himself an optimist about the long-term gains of “superintelligence”, as he insisted on calling it, put it another way: “We really don’t know what the market structure is going to be of these new technologies. Who’s going to get to make the money? What are the consequences for those that bet that they were going to make money, but the market structure doesn’t allow it?”

And AI is not just a stock market phenomenon but a huge driver of real-world exports, of the hardware and infrastructure necessary – albeit the benefits are heavily concentrated in a small number of economies, including Taiwan and South Korea. The knock-on effects, then, would be significant.

It is a familiar fear; but in its twice-yearly Global Financial Stability Review, the IMF laid out in detail the rising levels of debt being used to finance the AI boom; the intricate financial linkages between the companies involved; and the increasingly leveraged position of the investors – including hedge funds – backing them up.

As far back as the Wall Street crash of almost a century ago, the economist JK Galbraith was highlighting the fact that leverage – betting with borrowed money, effectively – tends to amplify booms and busts.

And as ministers met in the Thai capital, elsewhere in Asia there were tremors that may suggest Georgieva’s fear of “near-term disappointment” may already be gripping some investors.

South Korea’s Kospi share index recorded its biggest weekly loss since October 2008, at the height of the financial crisis, tumbling by 14.5% during the week, as traders ditched chip manufacturers such as Samsung and SK Hynix.

Analysts reported that questions around the borrowing, spending commitments and future profitability of AI companies unsettled the markets. Bonds issued by the datacentre CoreWeave slumped almost to distressed levels as these worries swirled.

Expectations of future increases in US interest rates also rose, after data showing that consumer price inflation rose in September, as did inflation at the US factory gate. US tech stocks were also hit, knocking 2% off the Nasdaq index between Monday and Thursday.

It was just the latest of a series of market wobbles of late, and finance ministers and central bankers probably gave it little thought as they were whisked in air-conditioned comfort back to their capitals this weekend.

But if the boom does turn to bust, sending shock waves through the global economy, they won’t be able to say they weren’t warned that the “resilience” we have been enjoying rests on shaky foundations.

stories.title: Burnham invites Swinney to work together on 'deeper Scottish devolution'
stories.summary: On his first substantive trip to Scotland since becoming PM, he says politicians should focus on solutions "right now" and move beyond the issue of Scottish independence.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Published 15 October 2026

The prime minister has invited the Scottish government to work together to put "power back in the hands" of regions - but insisted they must "move beyond" the constitutional question of Scottish independence.

Andy Burnham said he wanted to start work on a new deal for regional economic development in the next few months, including an offer of devolution from the Department for Work and Pensions (DWP).

Speaking at an event in Motherwell, Burnham called on first minister John Swinney to cede further powers from Holyrood to local areas before that happened.

SNP minister Stephen Flynn said the party had asked for increased devolution since the Smith Commission report was published in 2014.

The prime minister said devolution "was never supposed to stop at the doors of the Scottish Parliament" when Holyrood opened in 1999.

He said it was meant to be the "start of something deeper" where "communities had more of a say in their own future".

To play this video you need to enable JavaScript in your browser.

This video can not be played

Burnham invites Swinney to work together on 'deeper Scottish devolution'

However, he described Scotland as the most devolved nation in the UK but "one of the most centralised in Europe".

"During my first week in office, I told the first minister that I wanted to work with him to spread opportunities to communities across Scotland's regions and cities," he said.

"Through No10 North, we are rewiring the state and I want to make sure regions in Scotland are fully part of this.

"This is me making an offer to the Scottish government. With us working together, there is no limit to what we can achieve for the Scottish people."

Burnham to visit Scotland during SNP conference Published 4 days ago

Burnham - Rosebank and Jackdaw oil and gas decisions coming 'shortly' Published 3 days ago

The Scottish government set out plans for a radical rethink of the country's regional authorities last month.

A new two-tiered system would see the 32 local authorities replaced with six new regional authorities .

They would have power over major issues such as economic growth and education.

Below that, between 120 and 160 community authorities would govern more local issues, such as licensing and town centre improvements.

It would be the most significant change to Scotland's regional makeup since the current system was introduced by the UK government in 1996.

Burnham acknowledged that the Scottish government was working on local government reform, but said this had to "move faster".

It is not clear exactly what powers might be exercised at regional level other than employment support.

Burnham appears to expect the Scottish government to devolve some of its own powers to regional authorities.

But he made clear that he will not impose a model of regional devolution like the metropolitan mayors that already operate in England.

Instead he wants to try and agree a way forward with further discussions when the prime minister sits down with all the devolved first ministers at the end of this month.

John Swinney denied that too much power was centralised at Holyrood

Burnham also called for an end to "tribal politics" between the Scottish and UK governments.

He said he and Swinney "agreed on some things" but "didn't have to agree on everything".

Swinney is expected to promote his renewed push for independence in his keynote speech at the SNP conference on Saturday.

He previously welcomed Burnham telling MPs that a border poll would be considered in both Scotland and Northern Ireland if there was a clear consensus and public opinion had changed.

But Burnham later pushed back on that by telling Swinney at a meeting in Glasgow that a second Scottish independence referendum remains "off limits".

Asked whether devolving power more locally in Scotland would make independence more or less likely, the prime minister said: "I don't want to be the last PM of the UK.

"I just feel we all have to move beyond the constitutional questions.

"In my view, people in Scotland are suffering from the cost of living crisis, like they are in England and everywhere else, and I think our job is to focus on the practicalities, to focus on solutions for people right now."

He added: "Too much time is wasted on those dramas, it consumes too much energy."

'As many powers as possible'

Stephen Flynn - who was the SNP's leader at Westminster before becoming the Transport Secretary at Holyrood - said the Scottish government would welcome the opportunity to be handed more power over the country's economic prospects.

He said: "Interestingly the first minister sent a letter to the prime minister on Monday where he outlined a number of points he would like to see engagement on.

"This was number seven on that list, so we will of course engage with the prime minister fully in respect of his announcement today."

Before Burnham's speech, First Minister John Swinney said he was interested in "working constructively" with Westminster, adding he was "all for the Scottish Parliament having as many powers" as possible.

UK Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch said Burnham should be focusing on creating new opportunities in the energy sector.

She said: "This regional devolution plan is more jobs for the boys. What Andy Burnham should be doing is granting new oil and gas licences in the north sea."

"Devolution is a process, not a solution."

stories.title: Ex-top official Robbins reaches settlement with government over sacking
stories.summary: Sir Olly Robbins was sacked as the top civil servant in the Foreign Office over the vetting of Lord Mandelson.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Sir Olly Robbins was sacked as the top official in the Foreign Office in April

Published 16 October 2026

Sir Olly Robbins has reached an out-of-court settlement with the government, after he was sacked as the top civil servant in the Foreign Office over the vetting of Lord Mandelson to be US ambassador.

Sir Olly was fired by then Prime Minister Sir Keir Starmer earlier this year, after it emerged Lord Mandelson had been granted clearance for the role despite concerns being raised by vetting officials.

The FDA union, which represented him in the legal action, said Sir Olly had been made a "scapegoat" to "mask the misjudgement" of Sir Keir.

How much Sir Olly received in the settlement has not been made public.

It came after he requested a judicial review over the decision to dismiss him.

A government spokesperson said Sir Olly "had a distinguished public service career over three decades".

A statement added: "The government has reached a settlement with Sir Oliver following his dismissal. We will not be commenting further on HR matters."

Lord Mandelson was announced as the UK's ambassador to the US in December 2024, before in-depth vetting had been carried out, and formally took up the role in February 2025 after being granted security clearance.

Just seven months later, he was sacked after further information emerged about his previous friendship with the late convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.

Sir Olly was sacked in April, in the wake of a Guardian story that revealed the peer's security clearance had been granted despite vetting officials raising concerns, with the prime minister later saying he was "furious" he had not been informed at the time.

Sir Keir has previously said he sacked Sir Olly after not accepting his explanation for why clearance was granted, telling MPs in April: "I did ask him, and I did not accept his explanation. That is why I sacked him."

Sir Olly has since defended his role in the process, saying that the government's vetting processes must "remain absolutely confidential".

He previously told MPs that he had not seen the documentation from UK Security Vetting, the government's in-house vetting unit, containing their vetting assessment of Lord Mandelson.

He said that instead, he was given an oral briefing, during which he was told the vetting agency considered Mandelson to be a "borderline case", but that the Foreign Office may wish to grant clearance with "appropriate risk management".

Starmer sacks top Foreign Office official after Mandelson vetting revelations Published 17 April

Key evidence from sacked official at heart of Mandelson vetting row Published 21 April

Dave Penman, head of the FDA union, said: "This settlement may bring an end to the Judicial Review proceedings, but this whole unprecedented affair has damaged the bond of trust between civil servants and ministers, which is essential to the effective running of government.

"The scapegoating of Sir Oliver, to mask the misjudgement of the previous prime minister, marked one of the lowest points in the recent history of civil service-ministerial relations - which is quite the feat.

"We urge the government to clarify quickly the issues raised by this affair over ministerial involvement in the vetting process."

Sir Olly said: "I am grateful for all the support and good wishes from former colleagues, friends and strangers, which have helped me and my family during this difficult time.

"I want to thank the FDA for their assistance in reaching this settlement and I am looking forward to moving on to the next chapter of my life".

Sir Olly, who was appointed to the Foreign Office job in early 2025, has held a number of senior civil service roles and was previously the government's lead official during Brexit negotiations with the EU.

George Madgwick was featured in the ITV Exposure report on Reform candidates

Published 16 October 2026

A Reform councillor has accused ITV of "electoral interference" after undercover reporters joined its Portsmouth council election campaign as part of an undercover investigation into the party.

The ITV News Exposure documentary Undercover: A Year In Reform raised questions about Reform's vetting procedures for candidates following undercover filming.

The party's Hampshire leader George Madgwick was featured voicing support for the Portsmouth Patriots anti-immigration group. He subsequently issued a statement saying the undercover reporters potentially had an "impact on the result" of council elections.

ITV News has denied accusations of electoral interference. A spokesperson said the programme was produced in accordance with broadcasting regulations and was "in the public interest".

Reform has been under pressure following the two ITV News reports , which showed undercover footage, gathered over the past year, showing some of Reform's councillors and candidates using racist, violent and sexist language.

It comes two years after party leader Nigel Farage promised to root out "bad apples" from his party.

ITV News said it had reporters undercover with Reform UK candidates and councillors across England and Wales running up to the elections in May and four by-election campaigns this year and last.

The ITV Exposure documentary was produced by Hardcash Productions. The full 90-minute documentary - Undercover: A Year in Reform - is due to be broadcast on Sunday on ITV1 and ITVX.

A second ITV News report , external broadcast on Thursday showed footage of Madgwick admitting that the Portsmouth Patriots - members of whom were shown expressing far right views - were actively helping Reform to campaign in the run up to the council elections.

In a statement, he denied being a member of the group but said he had "supported their movement over the years from the sidelines".

Madgwick said the two undercover reporters campaigned with the party in Portsmouth in March and April.

"It leads me to wonder whether their interference in an election is a potential criminal offence."

"We have no way to know whether they posted flyers they were meant to. Or whether they gave us correct door knocking information," he said.

He said they had campaigned in four seats, three of which the party narrowly lost

"Their involvement would have had an impact on the result," he said.

He also said he was a "shocked and disgusted" the party had been "infiltrated" by the reporters.

"On a personal level I allowed these men in my home. I made them drinks. They met my dogs. It's an entirely disgusting invasion of personal privacy."

The Liberal Democrats took control of the council following the elections earlier this year, holding 22 seats, with Reform as the second-biggest party on 12 seats.

An ITV spokesperson said: "ITV's programme Undercover: A Year In Reform was produced in compliance with the Ofcom Broadcasting Code, relevant laws, and its broadcast is in the public interest.

"All journalists were instructed to operate within this framework and did so under the supervision of the programme's producers."

The Electoral Commission said it sets out details of electoral offences which relate to campaigning for agents and candidates.

"Our Code of Conduct for campaigners provides a guide to what is, and is not, acceptable behaviour."

"The consideration of any potential offences would be a matter for the police."

Loans made to property companies - including three controlled by Manchester City's Abu Dhabi owner - while Andy Burnham was Greater Manchester mayor are being investigated by councillors.

About 50 developers have been lent more than £1bn between them from a fund managed by the Greater Manchester Combined Authority (GMCA) since 2015.

John Leech, the chairman of the GMCA's Overview and Scrutiny Committee, told the BBC concerns had been raised about the transparency of the process to approve the loans.

"We just want to be clear that there is a transparent rather than an opaque process," said Leech, who is the Liberal Democrat opposition leader on Manchester City Council.

He said the approval process had been criticised as "very opaque in the past and that it's not necessarily been clearly understood why X was successful and Y wasn't".

A GMCA spokesperson said it was supporting the committee with its enquiries.

Downing Street did not comment.

The money came from the Greater Manchester Housing Investment Loan Fund (GMHILF).

The fund was set up in 2015 with an initial £300m of government investment to help developers build new homes across Greater Manchester.

Three property companies ultimately controlled by Manchester City owner Sheikh Mansour bin Zayed al Nahyan were granted loans worth about £55m in total.

The decisions to approve these loans were taken in 2017, in two meetings which were both chaired by Andy Burnham when he was mayor of Greater Manchester.

The decisions to grant loans from the fund were taken publicly by all members of the GMCA, not the mayor alone.

One of Manchester's leading property developers, Renaker, has received the majority of the £1bn lent out from the fund.

Renaker has been involved in a long-running legal battle over £140m worth of loans made to the developer through the GMCA's fund.

A rival developer, Aubrey Weis, claims the the loans were unfair subsidies.

In June, the Court of Appeal found there had been "no error of law" in the GMCA's decision to provide the loans but Weis is appealing the decision.

'Out of kilter'

The Overview & Scrutiny Committee, which reviews the activities of the mayor and the GMCA, agreed to launch an inquiry into the loans earlier this year and Leech is now taking that work forward, after being elected chairman recently.

Leech, a former Lib Dem MP in Manchester, said he felt the fund was intended to be for property companies struggling to access financing.

In 2015, when the loan scheme was launched, Bill Enevoldson, the GMCA's chief investment officer, said , external : "It is not designed to finance unviable projects but can unlock currently unfundable ones."

An evaluation of the fund , external from 2025 said it was designed to provide loans for "projects which might otherwise struggle to secure financing".

Leech said it was "not unreasonable" to ask why seemingly successful businesses needed to borrow public money through this loan scheme.

"In the case of Abu Dhabi, you would imagine that they wouldn't have any problem accessing funds from elsewhere as well," Leech said.

"And so the process clearly does seem to be out of kilter with what the original stated aims were back in 2015."

Leech said the committee had asked GMCA officers to produce a report about the use of these funds.

He said the committee will ask officers questions about the fund at a private meeting, before potentially making recommendations to the Greater Manchester mayor.

The committee does not have the power to sanction the mayor but it can investigate, require answers, expose problems and challenge decisions.

The committee could call forward witnesses, such as current Greater Manchester Mayor Bev Craig, to give evidence as part of the inquiry.

Conservative shadow sports minister Louie French said Burnham had "serious questions to answer" about the loans.

French said "taxpayers deserve transparency over how this money was awarded".

Manchester's relatively strong economic record has been driven in part by a property boom

In a statement, the GMCA said the funding for the loans had been lent "at commercial rates" and had delivered "11,000 new homes and regenerating brownfield land across the city region".

The GMCA said "not a single viable scheme was ever turned down".

A GMCA spokesperson added: "The fund is open to all developers, with lending criteria based on parameters set by the government and developed with external financial experts to reflect due diligence standards in the private sector.

"Every penny loaned from the fund is being fully repaid, delivering billions of pounds worth of development at no cost to the taxpayer."

In 2014, Manchester City Council and Abu Dhabi United Group, which owns Manchester City FC, formed a joint venture called Manchester Life.

Abu Dhabi United Group and Manchester Life were involved in three property developments that were partially financed through the GMCA's loan fund.

A Manchester Life spokesperson said: "It is standard for property development to be funded through a combination of investor equity and borrowing.

"All three sites had previously been derelict. The loans were provided on commercial terms and have been repaid in full, including interest."

The BBC asked Renaker for comment but it did not respond before publication.

Julia Hatmaker, the editor of the Place North West property news website, said viability was "always a struggle" in the development world.

She said the GMCA's loan scheme had been successful in building more homes in the city and generating a return on that investment.

But she said it's a "good time for the combined authority to re-evaluate what kind of project it wants to support with similar loan programmes and whether it wants to put stricter rules in place as to what developments can benefit from them".

stories.body:
British government must however align with the European Union’s position over tariffs on Chinese EVs

France has dropped its opposition to the UK being included in the EU’s “Made in Europe” legislation as long as the British government aligns with the bloc’s position over tariffs on Chinese EVs.

In a breakthrough for Andy Burnham, France on Thursday came round to backing Germany, which has always supported the UK’s calls to be designated European for the purposes of the Industrial Accelerator Act. The legislation, which is in its draft stage, is designed to protect domestic manufacturing from cheap Chinese competition.

According to a joint Franco-German paper seen by the Guardian, the two countries are now proposing that for the car industry specifically the UK could be included in Made in Europe.

“For the automotive sector, ‘Made in Europe’ should comprise the EU27 and an opt-in to further include European partners who were part of the EU single market as of 01/01/2020, subject to an agreement on full reciprocity – i.e. adopting the European preference scheme relevant to the automotive sector,” it says in a clear reference to the UK, which was still in the single market as an EU member in January 2020.

It would also include Norway, which is in the single market but not a member of the EU.

The paper added that the opt-in would come with conditions, including alignment on trade defence measures, which have included tariffs on Chinese EVs imposed by the EU in 2024 and any future trade barriers, such as the quota deal being finalised with China on its exports of hybrid cars.

The paper says that “as well as relevant anti-circumvention measures”, these “opt-in” countries would have to accept “dynamic alignment on the EU’s conditions related to third countries’ investments and on relevant EU trade defence measures”.

Liam Byrne, the chair of the UK’s business, innovation, science and trade committee, said he believed aligning with the EU on trade defence measures was a small price to pay to save British manufacturing.

“Sometimes politics is the least worst choice – aligning with Europe on trade defence against an over-subsidised China is the way we deliver for all of us,” he said.

“Tariffs on these would be a small price to pay for the protection of a European manufacturing industry which safeguards jobs across supply chains in the UK and makes us less prone to coercion from China in the future.”

On Wednesday the head of Mercedes implored EU leaders to let the UK join the package.

Locking the UK out of the EU’s flagship industrial Made in Europe legislation would amount to a “ deliberate choice” by EU leaders to “hurt” the car industry across the bloc, the head of Mercedes-Benz said.

The UK has been under pressure for weeks to align with the EU on tariffs on Chinese vehicles, but this week the business secretary Jonathan Reynolds said he would not be coerced into aligning with the EU’s policy.

However the government has been desperate to be included in the Made in Europe package, fearing billions of pounds of trade in the car industry could be lost if the UK was locked out of supply chains in the EU.

Earlier on Thursday trade minister Anas Sarwar hinted that the UK was minded to align on tariffs.

He told Politico the UK and the EU must “work together and act in lockstep” to tackle China’s dominance in the automotive sector.

Bernd Lange, the chair of the European parliament’s influential international trade committee, told the Guardian the UK should “of course” be included in the Made in Europe legislation, calling France’s opposition “not rational”.

A Downing Street spokesperson said it had yet to see the detail but saw the development as positive. “This is a Franco-German proposal and there is still a European process to run, but if confirmed, we welcome the objective to have UK included in the Industrial Accelerator Act and this would be good news for the British automotive industry and the jobs and investment it supports across the UK.”

stories.title: Labour calls for M4 relief road, seven years after axing the plan
stories.summary: Seven years after the party axed the project, Labour says the Welsh government should build the road.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
The former Welsh Labour government axed the plans in 2019

Published 15 October 2026

Labour's Welsh leader has called for the Plaid Cymru administration to start work on an M4 relief road - seven years after his party had axed it.

Ken Skates told BBC Wales that there was "no other option on the table" to solve congestion in Newport, and has backed a version of the original plan with changes.

The move will be seen by some as an attempt to distance Welsh Labour from part of the legacy of former First Minister Mark Drakeford.

Labour will table a vote in the Senedd on Wednesday calling for an "appropriate relief road" to be built.

A report said the road could now cost £3bn to build. Plaid Cymru accused Labour of hypocrisy.

Skates' announcement comes weeks after the Welsh government set out some options for tackling congestion , including proposals to close junctions in Newport.

It also means that all opposition groups - Reform, Labour and the Tories - are in favour of a relief road.

Drakeford axed previous proposals for an M4 Relief Road in 2019 - on the grounds of cost and the impact on the environment.

The Welsh government could close junction 27 at High Cross, and eastbound slip roads at junctions 25 and 26

The Welsh government has also commissioned an 18-month project to assess possible "roads-based" solutions - although it has ruled out the black route.

A report published earlier in October set out a number of alternatives to a new motorway, and said the relief road could cost around £3bn.

It also warned that the route was no longer safeguarded through the planning system.

"Over time, new development or other land use changes may occur within parts of the former corridor, making it progressively more difficult or expensive to deliver the same highway alignment in the future," it said.

But Ken Skates said the report "shows that no single or combined solution will adequately alleviate congestion on the M4 around Newport.

"That means that there is no other option on the table other than a relief road if we wish to solve the problem of congestion on that route."

He said he believed that an amended version of the original black route - the proposed motorway south of Newport that had been examined and backed by a public inquiry in 2019 - should be the road that got built.

Skates had served as transport minister under four Labour first ministers

The Welsh Labour leader said the proposed blue route alternative - using existing roads in part - was not appropriate.

"In reality, the black route remains the only appropriate route," Skates said.

"Further work would have to be undertaken to make sure that all environmental concerns today are met and adequately responded to, but something has to be done about congestion."

'We're a world away from 2019'

Asked what he would say to accusations of a U-turn, Skates added: "Well, it's a world away from where we were in 2019.

"Back then, we had come out of the EU, Brexit was causing enormous concern, we were planning for a no deal.

"We were... almost a decade into austerity. There was simply not the sort of money that was required to build the black route available to the Welsh government.

"It was right not to go ahead with it at the time because of the financial cost. I do believe firmly that had we gone ahead with it, it would have been paused or cancelled during Covid."

Skates said he wanted to know from the Welsh government what the status was now of the protected route for the relief road - which was ditched after the scheme was axed.

In a debate on 29 September, Deputy Transport Minister Mark Hooper said the black route was not achievable.

"The protected route status went when it was cancelled," he said.

"So, we're talking about decades of work to even get that off the ground."

Skates spoke ahead of the Co-operative Movement conference on Saturday, where he will say that people in the region "should be trusted, empowered and respected in deciding what affects them".

"Their need for congestion to be dealt with can only realistically be met through getting to work on a relief road.

"The debate over an appropriate solution and the balancing of environmental, human and economic concerns should be led by the people of the region, who know best what is needed in and for their communities."

Local Plaid Cymru MS, Peredur Owen Griffiths, who represents Casnewydd Islwyn, said Labour's "hypocrisy is astounding".

"It's as if they've forgotten they were in government for 27 years and scrapped plans to address the issue of congestion in and around Newport - only to now U-turn in opposition," he said.

"Plaid Cymru is clear that doing nothing isn't an option... the action we're considering could reduce traffic by 10% in just four years," he said.

stories.title: Damages for Greens deputy over false disorder claims
stories.summary: Mothin Ali is handed damages over claims made by a TV presenter and a social media commentator.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Mothin Ali will receive 'substantial damages' over the defamatory posts

Published 16 October 2026

A TV presenter and a social media commentator have apologised and will pay damages to the deputy leader of the Green Party after wrongly suggesting he participated in disorder.

Mothin Ali, a councillor on Leeds City Council, attended the 2024 Harehills unrest to assist police and appeal for calm, but posts on social media accused him of taking part in the trouble, the High Court heard.

Ali sued GB News presenter Alex Armstrong and social media commentator Bernadette Spofforth for defamation over posts on X. Both have apologised and agreed to pay "substantial damages".

Speaking outside court, Ali said: "The harm is already done. The smears leave their stench, even when proven to be false."

Trouble erupted in Harehills on the evening of 18 July 2024 after police helped social workers who were taking four children into emergency foster care.

Hundreds of people took to the streets, with a police car flipped over and a double-decker bus torched.

"I tried my absolute best to calm tensions, to protect police officers," said Ali, who has been deputy leader of the Green Party of England and Wales since 2025.

"I stayed on the scene to calm rioters and to reassure residents while buses burned. I stayed there to limit the damage, to limit the harm to my community.

"For my service to my community, I was not only accused of rioting, but something I take even more seriously - my honesty was brought into question."

A torched double-decker bus has become an enduring image of the Harehills unrest

As a result of the negative coverage, Ali said he was "harassed for days and weeks" and his family "lived in fear".

His car was also damaged.

"The context of this is how black and brown people are treated when they enter public life," he told reporters gathered outside the court.

Samantha Thompson, who represented Armstrong and Spofforth, a businesswoman from the Chester area, said the pair "apologise to the claimant for the serious harm to his reputation and his distress".

Green Party leader Zack Polanski said Ali was a "hero" for his actions on the night, adding: "He did exactly what an excellent councillor would do, working to calm down and heal division, and was praised across party lines at the time for doing so."
