stories.body:
Finance ministers gathering for the IMF annual meeting know the need for multilateral cooperation to deal with many crises. There is little chance of that

N ot much has gone right for the global economy this year, and plenty has gone wrong. Two big regional wars are destabilising prices and supply chains everywhere. Businesses and consumers are feeling the effects of a serious energy shock. Rising inflation has made it a lot more expensive for governments to finance their debts. China and the US are at loggerheads over trade.

Yet, so far, the impact has been modest. It is something of a miracle that the finance ministers and central bank governors gathered for this year’s annual meeting of the International Monetary Fund (IMF) in Bangkok are not having to deal with a full-blown crisis. This is not like the autumn of 2008, when the meetings took place during the worst of the global banking meltdown.

The IMF is right when it says countries have shown resilience when having to cope with so many headwinds. It could have been worse. A lot worse. There was even some good news for the UK, with the IMF upgrading its growth forecast for this year and praising the government for its deficit-reduction plan.

The better-than-expected performance of the global economy breaks with historical precedent. In the past, oil shocks of the magnitude witnessed since the start of Iran war have had a marked and immediate impact, but there are three key reasons why growth has remained robust and inflationary pressure has been muted this time.

The first is the massive amount of investment in the development of artificial intelligence. This has been particularly important in the US, which is comfortably the fastest growing member of the G7 group of major developed economies year on year. The second is that countries have drawn on inventories of oil, and that has helped to alleviate the loss of crude from the Middle East. Had stockpiles not been run down, oil prices would have risen even more sharply. The third is that China’s economic strategy relies on exporting cheap goods to the rest of the world, and this is bearing down on the prices of imports elsewhere.

All that said, the potential flashpoints for trouble are everywhere. The situation in the Middle East is deteriorating, with the conflict spreading to Saudi Arabia. Oil stocks are running low and Donald Trump has got the US into just the sort of forever war that he used to rail against. The downside to cheap Chinese goods is that they are threatening manufacturing jobs in the west, with Germany especially vulnerable.

Meanwhile, massive US investment in AI has pushed up the cost of borrowing and resulted in shortages of capital for non-AI sectors. Governments are coming under pressure to rein in spending or raise taxes in the hope that bond markets will be impressed by their efforts to cut budget deficits.

Warnings from (among others) the head of the IMF , Kristalina Georgieva, and the governor of the Bank of England , Andrew Bailey, of the need to run a tighter fiscal ship come at a time when voters want politicians to do more, not less. There is little appetite for a new era of austerity, and finance ministers know it. If they follow through on the tough talk and actually deliver painful measures, the backlash is likely to be brutal.

Just as big a problem for governments is the need – at a time when global supply chains are stretched and fragile – to boost national self-sufficiency. The student protests in India and France highlight the pressures on states to intervene. Yet the capacity of states to act effectively is much weaker than they care to admit.

At a time when globalisation is in retreat, there is a need for a strong system of multilateral cooperation to cope with the strains. That is not currently the case. The World Trade Organization is moribund in this new age of protectionism, and the IMF and the World Bank are reluctant to call Trump out for his erratic behaviour.

Yet the idea that a new era of partnership will flower when there is a new US president is for the birds. The problems of multilateralism run far deeper than that. The liberal world order that the IMF and World Bank have presided over since the end of the second world war was dysfunctional long before Trump arrived in office.

As the former UN official Richard Kozul-Wright points out in a paper published next month, the IMF and World Bank – created at the 1944 Bretton Woods conference – may still be operational but they have lost their connection to the New Deal principles laid out 82 years ago: state intervention in the running of economies, active industrial policy, the pursuit of full employment and help for poor countries to develop. “Instead, they have in recent decades pursued an agenda which encourages footloose capital, bolsters (and protects) private profit, and reduces the policy space available to governments. As a result, they have acted as hand maidens to an age of rising inequality, debt distress and heightened anxiety.”

after newsletter promotion

The IMF’s own programmes for countries that come looking for financial assistance illustrate Kozul-Wright’s point about the lack of policy space . Help comes with strings attached: an insistence on tax increases and spending cuts that are frontloaded so that half the measures are implemented in the first year and two-thirds within two years.

The IMF argues that this “tough love” has a higher chance of success, although its view of what constitutes success is limited, and primarily means that a borrowing country doesn’t need another IMF programme in the next three years. It doesn’t mean living standards are improving or that fewer people are in poverty.

Clearly it would help to return to New Deal principles. It would mean governments had more policy space to develop strategies tailored to their own needs. It would mean a boost to public investment. It would mean a new Marshall plan to help poorer countries cope with the climate crisis. It would mean a serious attempt to tackle debt distress. But, in all honesty, none of that has a chance of happening any time soon. As a result, the world will become hotter, more fractured, more prone to conflict, less equal and a lot angrier.

The IMF is worried that the limits of this resilience may soon be tested , and it is right to be worried. Peace in the Middle East would bring oil prices tumbling down, but unless that happens quickly a long winter lies ahead. This looks more like a crisis postponed than a crisis permanently avoided. A lull before the storm, in all probability.

Larry Elliott is a Guardian columnist

stories.body:
IMF: UK should cut spending rather than raise taxes on banks

Heather Stewart is the Guardian’s economics editor, reporting from Bangkok this week:

We’ve just been in the IMF’s Europe press conference, where the topic of bank taxes in the UK came up [following our report that the chancellor is poised to tax Britain’s banks].

Asked about the possibility at John Healey’s upcoming budget, Helge Berger , the economist who is deputy director in the IMF’s European department, suggested there might be better places to look to balance the books.

Berger pointed out that Healey’s predecessor, Rachel Reeves , had raised taxes in her budgets, saying:

double quotation mark “The last two budgets involved increasing government revenue, and ultimately there’s a moment where this becomes less productive but there’s still areas where Britain can make additional headroom available: modernising the property taxes or VAT, these are good examples. We wouldn’t recommend labour tax.”

Berger added:

double quotation mark “Ultimately, with taxes roughly at 40% of GDP - historically, for Britain, a high number - then of course balancing these measures on the fiscal side, doing a bit more there, makes good sense.”

He pointed to cost-cutting measures including removing the pensions triple lock , and “better targeting social benefits,” adding, “so I think that’s where you would put the emphasis, rather than the tax that you mentioned.”

Closing post

Time to wrap up…

The International Monetary Fund has urged John Healey to target savings on pensions and welfare, instead of taxing Britain’s banks at the budget later this month.

Helge Berger , deputy director of the IMF’s European department, was asked about bank taxes after the Guardian revealed Healey plans to tap the sector for additional revenue.

Berger replied that given the UK’s historically high tax-to-GDP ratio, it might be better to “put the emphasis” on cuts.

He said if additional tax revenue were needed, reforming property taxes or VAT might be a good place to start.

He added:

double quotation mark “Ultimately, with taxes roughly at 40% of GDP – historically, for Britain, a high number – then of course balancing these measures on the fiscal [spending] side, doing a bit more there, makes good sense.”

More here :

Berger’s comments came as shares in some UK banks dropped today, as traders anticipated a tax hit in the budget. Lloyds Banking Group and NatWest both fell by around 1%.

News of Healey’s plans provoked a backlash from some quarters.

The CBI said the chancellor should:

double quotation mark avoiding further sector-specific taxation, including on a banking sector already facing a higher tax rate than competing international financial centres.”

City analysts also warned that a new bank tax raid might weigh on the stock market , or hurt pensioners who rely on bank dividends for income .

In other news:

FTSE 100 closes higher despite bank tax worries

The London stock market has closed higher tonight, despite the threat of new bank taxes looming over the City.

The FTSE 100 shares index has ended the day up 41.5 points, or 0.4%, at 10,881 points.

Bank stocks recovered some of their earlier fall, but NatWest finished the session down 1.2% with Lloyds Banking Group down 0.95%.

The Footsie benefited from investors looking to avoid the sell-off in technology stocks – the US Nasdaq index is down 1% so far today.

Healey "considers new UK investor visa for wealthy foreigners"

Bloomberg are reporting this afternoon that Chancellor of the Exchequer John Healey is considering introducing a new UK visa route for wealthy foreigners.

The goal would be to attract immigrants who can help spur economic growth.

Proposals under considerion, they say, include a visa program directing immigrants to invest in innovative and high-growth sectors. Applicants might also be able to pay a flat-rate tax in exchange for investing in “qualifying investments”.

Bloomberg’s Lucy White reports:

double quotation mark One option being considered by Healey’s team is a proposal by the Institute for Public Policy Research, which recommends a visa program directing immigrants to invest £5 million ($6.7 million) over five years in a vehicle overseen by the state-owned British Business Bank. The pooled funds would be directed into innovative and high-growth sectors and pay out a set rate of return “significantly lower than market rates.” Under another proposal by lobby group Foreign Investors for Britain, applicants would pay £2.5 million minimum into “qualifying investments” such as those run by the BBB. In return, they’d be allowed to pay an annual flat-rate tax of £200,000 for up to 15 years.

US industrial production up 0.7% in September

The latest US economic data shows America’s economy is continuing to grow, thanks in part to the AI boom.

US industrial production rose 0.7% in September, beating expectations, led by investment in AI infrastructure, energy security and advanced manufacturing.

That follows a 0.1% rise in August.

Elsewhere in the markets, the US dollar has dipped after Federal Reserve chair Kevin Warsh resisted hinting that his central bank might raise interest rates later this month.

Warsh declined to give any guidance about the Fed’s next move, during his appearance at the IMF’s Annual Meeting today, saying only:

double quotation mark “We made very clear that we would deliver price stability, and we removed a dose of accommodation about a month ago. I don’t prejudge meetings. I don’t believe in saying now what I might do at the meetings that we have in the balance of this year.”

The pound is now up almost a whole cent against the dollar, at $1.336.

CoreWeave shares down again amid AI debt worries

Over on Wall Street, shares in AI company CoreWeave have tumbled again at the start of trading, as concerns grow over its borrowing levels.

CoreWeave are leading the fallers on the Nasdaq index, down 7%.

Yesterday, the cost of protecting CoreWeave bonds against default rose to the highest intraday level on record.

CoreWeave runs AI datacentres, funded by issuing high-yield debt.

Shares in CoreWeave fell sharply earlier this week – including a 15% tumble on Wednesday – before recovering some ground yesterday after Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang voiced support for the company.

Fawad Razaqzada, market analyst at StoneX, says:

double quotation mark CoreWeave was among the names caught up in the recent sell-off, although the stock recovered yesterday after Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang said the company’s financial position was improving and its cost of capital was falling. That is hardly an impartial endorsement, given Nvidia’s sizeable interest in CoreWeave, so the more important question is whether the recovery can be sustained once the immediate reassurance fades. More broadly, this week’s price action suggests the market debate is beginning to shift. The question is no longer simply how large the AI opportunity can become, but how profitable the enormous investment required to realise it will ultimately be.

The head of ⁠the IMF on Friday isued an appeald to global leaders to cooperate in the face of multiple economic risks, such as rapid advances in AI and the Iran war.

Kristalina Georgieva said the sheer speed of technological change added to the long list of challenges, including disruptions to the global trading ​system, high food and energy prices and lingering wars, all of which threatened to widen the ‌gulf between advanced economies and the world’s poor.

Bond markets, ‌she said, were clearly sensing the risks, with US, German and Japanese 10-year sovereign yields reaching their highest levels in decades.

“The need of the hour is for urgent and practical international cooperation,” Georgieva told at a plenary session today.

Audit, tax and business advisory firm, Blick Rothenberg argues that increasing the bank corporation tax surcharge from 3% back to 8% might backfire.

Artur Vorobyev , a director at Blick Rothenberg, says:

double quotation mark Although this may sound like a reversal of a tax cut, when the surcharge was reduced in 2023, corporation tax increased from 19% to 25%. The combined rate on bank profits went up from 27% to 28%. Increasing the surcharge to 8% now would bring the combined rate to 33%. This is a significant rise and is counterproductive if the Government wants banks to invest and lend more to aid growth.”

Bloomberg: UK banks warn Healey’s tax plan will curtail economic growth

Bloomberg are reporting that the UK’s banking industry has “ramped up lobbying” against extra taxes planned by Chancellor of the Exchequer John Healey.

They are apparently warning that a hike could shrink economic output by £6bn over five years and hit areas outside London the hardest.

Bloomberg add:

double quotation mark Pushing a surcharge banks pay on top of a standard corporation tax to 8% from 3% would also cut lending by about £10 billion by 2029 and reduce investment into the UK, according to a letter sent earlier this week to Healey by David Postings, chief of industry lobby group UK Finance .

[£6bn, incidentally, is also an estimate for the amount of tax lost over the last three years from the cut in the bank surcharge to 3% ….]

Photos: Protests at the IMF

Demonstrators have been protesting against the IMF and the World Bank at their meeting in Bangkok today, for the second day running.

According to the Bangkok Post , they encountered a police blockade which prevented them walking to Queen Sirikit National Convention Center, where the annual meetings are being held.

The Assembly of the Poor put the number of local and international protesters at 1,000 but the Metropolitan Police Bureau estimated about 800.

IMF: UK should cut spending rather than raise taxes on banks

Heather Stewart is the Guardian’s economics editor, reporting from Bangkok this week:

We’ve just been in the IMF’s Europe press conference, where the topic of bank taxes in the UK came up [following our report that the chancellor is poised to tax Britain’s banks].

Asked about the possibility at John Healey’s upcoming budget, Helge Berger , the economist who is deputy director in the IMF’s European department, suggested there might be better places to look to balance the books.

Berger pointed out that Healey’s predecessor, Rachel Reeves , had raised taxes in her budgets, saying:

double quotation mark “The last two budgets involved increasing government revenue, and ultimately there’s a moment where this becomes less productive but there’s still areas where Britain can make additional headroom available: modernising the property taxes or VAT, these are good examples. We wouldn’t recommend labour tax.”

Berger added:

double quotation mark “Ultimately, with taxes roughly at 40% of GDP - historically, for Britain, a high number - then of course balancing these measures on the fiscal side, doing a bit more there, makes good sense.”

He pointed to cost-cutting measures including removing the pensions triple lock , and “better targeting social benefits,” adding, “so I think that’s where you would put the emphasis, rather than the tax that you mentioned.”

IG have spotted that UK traders are increasingly betting against the big four British banking stocks ahead of the Autumn Budget.

Data from their trading platform shows that the number of short trades across the big 4 banks increased by 58% week on week.

Barclays saw the sharpest increase in selling activity, with short trades jumping 81% week-on-week.

XTB: Bank tax could hurt FTSE 100

Higher taxes on banks could have an impact on the FTSE 100 since the banking sector makes up nearly 20% of the UK blue chip shares index, says Kathleen Brooks , research director at XTB.

double quotation mark The UK’s banking sector has been extremely resilient this year and has performed positively, for example Lloyds Banking Group is higher by 20% in the past 12 months. The risk is that downward pressure will now build, and this will dim the attractiveness of the entire index. We will need to wait for the Budget to get the details of this tax, afterall, this is the Labour Party and they are well known for their U-turns. The Chancellor may need to water down plans for a tax if he wants to avoid denting both the economy and the FTSE 100.

Back in Bangkok, IMF chief Kristalina Georgieva has warned that the risks of artificial intelligence may exceed its opportunities if no adequate safeguards and ethical framework are put in place.

During a panel discussion that included Anthropic co-founder Jack Clark , Georgieva said AI was already strengthening the global economy, but could also deliver negative shocks if it failed to deliver major productivity gains as quickly as hoped, Reuters reports .

Georgieva says:

double quotation mark “If there are no safeguards, then the risks may exceed the opportunities. And above all, we do need an ethical foundation, and I’m not sure we are there as a society.”

Pound at three-week high

The pound has touched its highest level against the US dollar in over three weeks.

Sterling has gained half a cent to $1.3335, its highest level since 23 September.

Traders are expecting the Bank of England to raise interest rates in November – higher rates are typically good for a currency’s value.

Investors will also be weighing up the impact of the budget later this month – and wondering whether John Healey will maintain the UK’s fiscal headroom – the buffer for meeting its borrowing rules.

Matthew Ryan , head of market strategy at global financial services firm and FX specialists Ebury , says:

double quotation mark “The question that matters most to us is how the budget could affect the pound and the gilt market. We see the fallout in markets as dependent on whether Healey can keep the economic damage to a minimum, while convincing markets that future spending plans won’t come at the expense of debt sustainability.”

Pensioners could suffer if the government hikes taxes on banks, points out Russ Mould, investment director at AJ Bell :

double quotation mark “The government might argue that banks are doling out significant amounts of money in dividends to shareholders, implying there is plenty of scope for them to pay a little bit more tax. The flipside is that any hit to dividends to offset higher taxes would penalise the large number of people in retirement who invest in banking shares for income.

No sign of a rebound in UK bank shares yet – Lloyds (now down 2.2%) are still the biggest faller on the FTSE 100, with NatWest now off 2%.

In other banking news, the UK government reportedly tried to persuade UBS to shift its headquarters and stock market listing to London in the event of the bank relocating out of Switzerland.

The FT has the story :

double quotation mark Rachel Reeves pitched London as a potential new home for UBS in discussions with the bank’s chair Colm Kelleher during her time as chancellor, according to people briefed on the talks. The pair discussed the possibility of UBS moving its legal headquarters and listing to the UK if it were to redomicile, the people added, with the most recent meeting taking place earlier this year.

Will Howlett , financials analyst at Quilter Cheviot , points out that the jump in bank profits means tehy can absorb higher taxes.

He also suggests that higher bank taxes are already ‘priced in’ to the company’s share prices, saying:

double quotation mark “With the runup to the Budget and the rumour mongering that comes with it now in full flow, the government seems to be giving the UK’s banking sector some mixed messages. John Healey has called the UK’s banks a ‘jewel in the crown of the economy’, yet briefings suggest they are going to get hit by a fresh increase in the levy on its profits. “The banks did manage to escape such measures last year, but with higher interest rates now expected for longer, the government may be thinking now is the time they can strike, especially if they want to limit the number of personal taxes they go after at the budget. The government is facing increased fiscal pressure as a result of the Middle East shock, and while economic growth is solid just now, this would appear easier pickings to help bolster the public finances. “That said, much of this is reflected in valuations, with UK domestic banks already trading at a discount to European peers. That may explain the relatively muted reaction to share prices this morning. More domestically focused banks, like Lloyds and NatWest have seen drops in their share prices of around 2%, although this is far smaller than the approximately 6% hit you would see if the surcharge were raised by 5 percentage points back to the 8% where it stood previously. Much of the bad news is already priced in at a time where the banks are also able to absorb such a hit thanks to the profits they are making at the moment as a result of higher interest rates.

stories.body:
Meta says Muse excels at ‘multi-step reasoning’ and ‘complex software engineering’ as it races to catch up to Chinese rivals

Meta on Thursday launched a new open-weight AI model which it claims rivals, and in some cases outperforms, similar products from leading Chinese developers.

Muse Spark Open “is the most capable US open-weight model to date,” Meta’s chief of AI Alexandr Wang wrote on X.

Unlike so-called closed models – such as Anthropic’s Claude or OpenAI’s ChatGPT – developers can download the parameters, known as weights and biases, of an open-weight model and modify them.

Chinese developers have emerged as dominant players in the open-weight market for AI models over the past couple of years.

Alibaba’s Qwen, Moonshot AI’s Kimi K3 and Z.ai’s GLM models have been considered open-weight frontrunners globally, but Meta claims its new open model now competes on a similar level.

“Built for coding and agentic work,” Muse Spark Open “excels at long-horizon tasks, complex software engineering, and multi-step reasoning,” Meta said in a blogpost, adding that “strong safeguards” have been integrated into the new model.

Muse Spark Open is also “optimized” to run on Apple’s advanced M5 Ultra chips, Meta said, signaling an unusual partnership between the two tech companies.

Muse Spark Open requires significant computing power. Users can run the model on two Mac Studios with M5 Ultra chips to create a “supercomputer” on their own desktop, Meta said.

The launch comes just days after Meta announced its newest closed model, which it said rivalled the most advanced versions of ChatGPT and Claude.

Meta’s AI efforts were initially focused on open models, but more recently Zuckerberg has pushed the company to compete with OpenAI and Anthropic.

stories.title: We must save water as drought becomes new normal, says minister
stories.summary: Severe drought was declared across parts of southern England after months of low rainfall.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Severe drought conditions have been declared across parts of southern England

Published 16 October 2026

The government has warned action is needed to prevent water shortages becoming "the norm" after severe drought was declared across parts of southern England.

Water and flooding minister Emma Hardy told MPs current drought conditions were "something we have not experienced for decades" and urged people to "think about ways to use water wisely over the coming weeks".

Severe drought was declared across parts of southern England on Thursday after months of low rainfall, with around 50 million people now impacted.

Parts of Cornwall, Devon, Dorset, Somerset, East Sussex and West Sussex are all affected by the move announced by the Environment Agency.

The government said supplies would not be interrupted but declaring severe drought would ensure "proactive steps are taken to safeguard water before any disruption occurs".

Speaking in the House of Commons, Hardy said the measures were down to "exceptionally low rainfall" and depleted reservoir levels.

How we got to severe drought and what is next Published 1 day ago

Severe drought declared and hosepipe bans in force - is your area affected? Published 2 days ago

Drought permit issued in bid to secure supply Published 8 October

The minister noted Yorkshire also moved into drought status last week.

"That means over 80% of England is now in drought, affecting around 50 million people," she said.

"The South East and South West, in particular, have experienced their driest April to September in over a century.

"While the record-breaking heat and lack of rainfall have put our water resources under immense pressure this year, we must take action now to prevent this situation becoming the norm."

Robbie Moore, shadow minister for environment, food and rural affairs, accused the government of being "slow to react" to the conditions.

"This is the third drought in five years, it should not have caught the government off guard," he told MPs.

Hardy insisted "we know that this the new normal when it comes to our weather", adding: "This is exactly why we are preparing for it."

The latest figures , external for Wimbleball Reservoir on Exmoor show it is at 14.9% capacity, while Ardingly in West Sussex is 19.4% full. Other major reservoirs are also low, including Roadford in Devon at 36.8%, Burrator at 33.6%, Colliford in Cornwall at 35% and Stithians at 21.9%.

Wimbleball serves about 300,000 properties across east Devon, north Devon, Somerset, west Dorset and west Somerset, while Ardingly Reservoir supplies 280,000.

As part of the severe drought conditions, water companies have been asked to conduct daily monitoring of these reservoir levels along with tougher monitoring of water quality.

Wimbleball reservoir on Exmoor, now at just 14.9% capacity, provides water for about 390,000 people

The Environment Agency was also expected to increase compliance checks on businesses withdrawing water from natural sources to ensure they only take permitted quantities.

It said "small changes" including taking shorter showers, fixing leaks and turning off taps while brushing teeth could "make a real difference".

"These aren't token gestures," the agency said.

"They cut the amount of water we need to take from rivers and groundwater, protecting supplies for people and leaving more for wildlife, wetlands and the natural systems we all depend on."

The Environment Agency said further dry weather was expected for the rest of October: "The usual seasonal rainfall has yet to arrive, and 82% of England remains in drought."

In some areas, 120% of the expected rainfall was needed for the next six months or "drought conditions will continue and could worsen", it said.

Severe drought is the most serious level, and was declared "when evidence shows drought is causing, or will soon cause, serious harm, and that emergency action is needed to protect people, water supplies, the environment, farming, infrastructure or other critical services".

stories.title: Burnham asks for 'manual trawl' of records for former Man City links
stories.summary: The PM has faced fresh questions about hospitality dinners since the club was found guilty of Premier League rule breaches.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Andy Burnham has faced calls for transparency since his comments about Man City's owners shocked many in the world of football

Published 15 October 2026

Andy Burnham has said he has asked for a "manual trawl" of records relating to his previous contact with Manchester City football club.

The prime minister said on Thursday he had asked the Greater Manchester Combined Authority (GMCA) to search "everything" to ensure "full transparency".

He continues to face questions over any relations he had with Man City while mayor of Greater Manchester for almost a decade until June. The club has been found guilty of "systematically" breaking Premier League rules.

Declarations of Burnham's contact with the club were released on Monday, but confusion grew later when it emerged records of two dinners Burnham had with Man City's chairman had been deleted.

Speaking to broadcasters on Thursday, Burnham said of the GMCA: "I've asked them to do a more manual trawl of everything, as I want everything possible to be out there."

He insisted that the occasions he dined with Man City chairman Khaldoon Al Mubarak at matches at the Etihad in 2017 and 2018 were "included" in a statement issued by the local authority on Monday.

It comes after he was accused by his political opponents of seeking to cover up the meetings.

The GMCA statement , external mentioned a meeting Burnham had "informally" with Al Mubarak in the stands at a 2019 match, and a formal meeting the pair held at the UK Government's Global Investment Summit in October 2021, but did not specify the two dinners.

It went on: "In his capacity as Mayor, he was a guest of Manchester City FC at home matches on a small number of occasions [...]."

As mayor, Burnham previously declared the dinners from Man City, valued at a combined total of £1,000 for hospitality.

Man City chairman Khaldoon Al Mubarak (left) chats to Andy Burnham in 2019 at the Etihad Stadium, when he was mayor of Greater Manchester

But records of them have since been deleted from the GMCA website.

The BBC understands it is the authority's policy to only publish entries from the current mayoral term - but the authority has not clarified why the register dates back to 2022, despite the current mayoral term beginning in 2024.

It also remains unclear what, if anything of significance, was discussed at the two dinners.

A GMCA spokesperson said the authority was now carrying out a further manual trawl of Burnham's engagements with Manchester City during his time as mayor "and will provide the information to the prime minister to publish when completed".

Burnham has faced pressure since comments in a BBC interview in September , saying he would be "really concerned" if Man City's owners now sold the club, following an independent commission finding the club guilty of multiple Premier League financial rule breaches.

Tory leader Kemi Badenoch told him at Prime Minister's Questions this week that the issue was not "going away".

The commission found City had broken rules over a nine-year period to 2018 by creating "sham" contracts with commercial partners to secretly funnel more than £830m into football operations.

The findings have outraged many and left the top flight of English football in limbo with its top team facing potential sanctions. Man City continues to deny any wrongdoing and has lodged an appeal.

stories.title: Equality watchdog writes to Greens over 'Zionism is racism' motion
stories.summary: The party was reported to the Equality and Human Rights Commission by MPs and antisemitism campaigners.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Green leader Zack Polanski said the motion was 'imperfect' but supported the substance of it

Published 15 October 2026

The equality watchdog has written to the Green Party asking for more information about a controversial "Zionism is racism" motion passed by members.

The Equality and Human Rights Commission (EHRC) said it recognised that "many Jewish people will be feeling vulnerable" following the motion, passed at the party's conference earlier this month.

The motion described Zionism as an ideology supporting "an ethnonationalist Jewish state in historic Palestine to the exclusion and/or domination of the non-Jewish population".

In a response to the EHRC letter, the party said it "will not discriminate against or exclude people for holding Zionist views" and was committed to tackling antisemitism.

Dozens of Labour and Lib Dem MPs and Jewish campaigners wrote to the regulator raising concerns about antisemitism after the Green motion was passed.

Speaking at a press conference on Friday, author of the motion Lubna Speitan, said the Labour government had been a "participant in genocide" and had "no moral high ground to talk to us about antisemitism, racism or any other matter".

The International Court of Justice is currently hearing a case that accuses Israeli forces of genocide. Israel has said the accusations are "wholly unfounded" and based on "biased and false claims".

Speitan defended her motion arguing that it was "aimed at the political ideology and practice of Zionism as defined in the motion and not the religious or ethnic background of those who may identify as Zionism".

"Rejecting Zionism and supporting the liberation of Palestine is not discriminatory against Jewish people," she added.

Alongside Jewish groups, the motion was criticised by four of the five Green MPs and two former leaders, one of whom said it was "dangerous" and "divisive".

It piled some pressure on Green leader Zack Polanski in the wake of a by-election defeat. He said the motion was "imperfect" and he wanted to see it amended.

Labour has said it will end power-sharing agreements with the Greens on local councils, unless its councillors disown the motion.

On Thursday, the EHRC confirmed it had written to the Greens following the complaints received.

A spokesperson for the watchdog said: "We have written to the Green Party of England and Wales about its recently adopted 'Zionism is racism' motion to ask for more information and assess its practical implications and potential impact.

"We have received complaints alleging unlawful activity under the Equality Act 2010, including concerns that Jewish people could face discrimination because of their beliefs following the adoption of the motion."

The watchdog said it would "take action where appropriate" after assessing the extra information.

"In the case of the Green Party motion, compliance with the Equality Act is likely to hinge on the practical effects of the motion," the spokesperson added.

In a letter earlier this month , some MPs raised concerns not only about the motion itself but also amendments to protect Jewish Green members at Zionist synagogues being voted down.

"Taken together, these developments raise serious questions about whether Jewish members can participate freely and equally in the party, and whether their religious and communal connections could expose them to complaints or disciplinary action," their letter said.

Separately, the Campaign Against Antisemitism wrote to the EHRC alleging the party had breached the Equality Act through discrimination against Jews.

The campaign group said the motion "effectively states that the state of Israel should not exist" and "defines support for a Jewish homeland in any form as racist".

Having been backed by members, the motion has become party policy but will not necessarily be included in the party's manifesto at the next general election.

In response to the EHRC letter, the Green Party of England and Wales said it "will not discriminate against or exclude people for holding Zionist views" and the motion sets out a political position with "no impact on membership conditions or internal disciplinary processes".

"The party's comprehensive antisemitism guidance, which forms part of our framework of ethics, remains unchanged," a spokesperson added.

"We remain committed to tackling antisemitism and ensuring Jewish members feel welcome and respected."

stories.title: Banks expect to be hit with higher taxes in Budget
stories.summary: Senior banking executives have told the BBC they expect to be "on the menu" in the chancellor's Budget tax later this month.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Published 15 October 2026

Chancellor John Healey is planning to increase taxes on the bank sector, senior banking executives have told the BBC.

Healey has described banks as part of "the crown jewels" of the UK economy, but leaders in the sector have said it will be "on the menu" at the Budget in two weeks' time.

The biggest four banks collectively made about £15bn profit in the first six months of this year, and trade unions have called for them to face additional taxes.

The trade body for the banking sector, UK Finance, warned "further increases in bank taxes would weaken competitiveness, discourage investment and job creation, and work against the government's ambition to deliver growth in every postcode".

Shares in banks including Lloyds and NatWest fell on Friday on expectations that the sector would be hit by tax hikes. The firms were among the biggest fallers on the UK stock market, with both dropping more than 2%.

Barclays fell only slightly and HSBC actually rose as both have large international businesses and would be less affected by a hike in UK taxes.

What is the Budget and what could be in it?

There are a number of ways the chancellor could extract more money from the sector.

One option is for Healey is to reverse a reduction in the surcharge that banks pay on corporation tax, from 8% to 3%, introduced in 2023, by Conservative chancellor Jeremy Hunt.

Critics argue this would be unfair noting the cut coincided with a rise in corporation tax from 19% to 25%.

Healey could also raise the bank levy - a small percentage charged on loans.

The BBC understands that the Treasury is leaning towards changing the surcharge if they were to go ahead as it is easier to change an existing tax rather than impose a new windfall tax.

Reversing the 2023 surcharge rate would raise around £2bn. However, the last government was persuaded that adding 8% on top of corporation tax of 25% would leave UK banks struggling to compete with European and US rivals - so it may be that it is raised, but not all the way back to the 8% level.

Speaking to the press in Bangkok, Healey praised the role banks play in the British economy.

Adding that he has "decisions to take in the Budget", he said: "My observation on the banks is that people too often see ​them as big, distant financial institutions, when they are hardwired into the economic fabric of this country and our future ⁠prospects."

In the past banks have successfully argued that higher taxes would risk making the UK uncompetitive with other jurisdictions and would reduce their ability to lend, and therefore be anti-growth.

Sir Philip Augar, an author and former banker in the City of London, told the BBC's Today programme there was "room for a moderate increase" in taxes on the sector that could raise up to £3bn a year.

He said lenders were enjoying "booming conditions", benefiting from higher interest rates which boost their profits.

Rising interest rates have expanded the margin between the rate at which banks lend to customers and the rate they pay savers.

Sir Philip added that when the banking sector "hits really rocky times it expects the taxpayer to bail them out - when it hits boom times, it expects some kind of special treatment".

He said banks cannot simultaneously be "too big to fail and too big to tax".

Paul Nowak, general secretary of the Trades Union Congress, which represents trade unions, said Britain's four biggest banks are making a billion pounds a week, with bonuses at post-financial crash records. "These are bumper profits - driven by high interest rates and households' mortgage misery," he said.

"Now it's time to make sure banks pay their fair share," he added.

"But if the chancellor does ask the Banks to pay a fairer share of tax in the Budget, that's 100% the right call," he added.

Burnham announces scheme to help first-time buyers onto housing ladder Published 27 September

Healey says surprise UK growth is 'sign of resilience' ahead of Budget Published 2 days ago

Faisal Islam: What surprise praise for UK economy tells us about the Budget Published 3 days ago

Banks were pleased to have avoided being targeted at the last Budget, given the large profits they have made in recent years.

There is another option that has been discussed with Treasury officials. Currently banks can use losses from the past to offset against profits - thereby reducing their tax bill in any given year. Lloyds in particular has been a beneficiary of this policy, as large losses from the financial crisis have been used to lower tax bills ever since.

Some analysts and bank executives have pushed the idea of a moratorium on this practice for a few years, which would yield an estimated extra £1bn per year for the Treasury. That would provide a windfall while being "a lot more bearable", in the words of one bank executive.

It would also spare foreign banks from an additional hit, including JP Morgan, whose chief executive Jamie Dimon has warned that the UK already has one of the highest tax burdens on banks in the world. He warned that adding further sector-specific taxes could discourage investment and damage competitiveness.

However, industry leaders say any form of tax rise that hits UK banks and exempts foreign banks' operations in the UK would be hard to square with the government's push to back British business.

A Treasury spokesperson said: "As has always been the case, decisions on tax are a matter for the chancellor to set out at fiscal events, rather than routinely commenting on rumour, speculation or proposals."

stories.title: 'Massive challenge' to protect Donaldson from harm in jail
stories.summary: The former DUP leader was sentenced to 15 years for sex abuse against two women when they were children.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Donaldson, pictured leaving at court in June, will spend half of his 15-year sentence behind bars

Published 16 October 2026

Protecting convicted paedophile Jeffrey Donaldson from harm inside jail will be a "massive risk-management headache" for prison bosses, according to a former governor.

The ex-Democratic Unionist Party (DUP) leader was given a 15-year sentence on Thursday after being convicted of 18 counts of sex abuse, including rape , against two women when they were children.

He is serving his sentence at Maghaberry Prison near Lisburn but will spend only half of his term behind bars.

Ian Acheson, who worked for HM Prison Service for about a decade, said the former Lagan Valley MP faced risks from fellow inmates.

A prison van took Donaldson from Newry courthouse to jail after he was sentenced

Donaldson represents a "very complex challenge to the Northern Ireland Prison Service", Acheson added.

"There are always hierarchies within prisons - and there are even hierarchies within sex offenders - and the lowest of the low and the most vulnerable in terms of hostility from others are those who've been convicted of sexual violence against a minor," he said.

But he said it would also be necessary to "examine potential political or sectarian targeting" relating to Donaldson's leadership of the DUP and his service in the Ulster Defence Regiment, a former Army unit.

"The prison has a duty of care to protect him and he is uniquely vulnerable," Acheson told BBC Radio Ulster's Talkback programme.

"Maghaberry, in previous inspections, has indicated that it operates an integrated regime, where sex offenders can be safely managed in the wider prison community.

"I don't think that is remotely viable for Jeffrey Donaldson, given those offence characteristics and his background.

"So either he is kept, in effect, in conditions of solitary confinement for years and years or another solution has to be found.

"I don't think it's acceptable to keep him in conditions of solitary confinement - it may not even be legal."

Reading in his cell

Donaldson spends up to 18 hours a day in his cell at Maghaberry Prison, which holds about 1,600 inmates.

It is thought he has been put in the Moyola Unit, which primarily houses prisoners with health issues, for his own safety as it isolates him from risk of attack or verbal abuse from other prisoners.

He is believed to spend much of his day reading books from the prison library.

Acheson said the disgraced former politician was "entitled to protection but he's not entitled to special, preferential treatment".

There was a "precedent within the UK" to transfer prisoners within different jurisdictions, Acheson added - therefore Donaldson "could be potentially compulsorily transferred" to another jail.

Donaldson was convicted in June of sex offences against two females referred to in his trial as Victim A and Victim B.

He was sentenced to 11 years for his crimes against Victim B and four years for offences against Victim A.

He will also be required to sign the Sex Offenders Register for life.

During sentencing, Judge Paul Ramsey said Donaldson's crimes had led to a "catastrophic descent into disgrace".

Donaldson, who denied the charges, is seeking to appeal his convictions .

Should his attempt to appeal fail, he will be released from prison at the end of 2033.

He qualifies for a 50% remission in his sentence because the offences were committed before the Criminal Justice (Northern Ireland) Order 2008 came into effect.

The remainder of his sentence will be served under supervision in the community on licence.

Who is Jeffrey Donaldson?

Donaldson's time in politics began in 1985 when he was elected for the Ulster Unionist Party (UUP) as a member of the Stormont assembly for South Down.

In 1997, Donaldson became the MP for Lagan Valley, representing the UUP. He would remain an MP until 2024.

However, in 2003 he quit the UUP and defected to the DUP.

Donaldson was awarded a knighthood in the 2016 Queen's Birthday Honours list, and, in 2021, became leader of the DUP .

He remained the party's leader until March 2024, when he was charged with a series of historical sexual offences against children .

After his conviction this year, Donaldson asked for his knighthood to be forfeited and tendered his resignation from the Privy Council with immediate effect.

In July, King Charles stripped Donaldson of his knighthood .

stories.title: Reform faces questions over candidate vetting after undercover filming
stories.summary: Reform UK says the party has "improved and prioritised its vetting procedures".
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Published 16 October 2026

Reform UK is facing further questions about its vetting procedures for candidates, after undercover filming broadcast by ITV News , external .

In the film, gathered over the course of a year, an undercover reporter is advised by a local party chairman to delete social media posts supportive of far-right activist Tommy Robinson, before being encouraged to apply to stand to be a councillor for the party.

It also shows a former Reform candidate claiming he failed the party's vetting process twice but was still allowed to stand to be a councillor. Reform denies the individual failed vetting in the first place.

Reform said the party had "improved and prioritised its vetting procedures".

In a statement, the party said that "from time to time, a handful of individuals who do not share our values will initially make it through vetting" but added: "This is the same for all organisations."

It follows undercover filming broadcast on Wednesday night, which showed some of Reform's councillors and candidates using racist, violent and sexist language .

Reform MP Robert Jenrick said all political parties had "bad apples".

Speaking to the BBC's Today programme, he said he "didn't like what I heard in the documentary" but argued that the party had acted quickly, removing or suspending those in the undercover film.

"I don't accept this happens any more in Reform than in any other party," he added.

The party said: "There is no room for racism in Reform UK. We always respect due process of investigations and whilst these are ongoing it would not be appropriate to comment on individual cases."

Reform also accused the ITV investigation of "extreme methods of deception" and using false information to obtain an undercover role in Reform's headquarters.

Jenrick said he believed the undercover reporters had wanted to find evidence of party leader Nigel Farage "acting in an inappropriate way" but had not succeeded.

Two years ago, Farage vowed to vet candidates more "rigorously", after the party dropped a series of candidates following reports they had made offensive or racist comments.

However, the party has continued to face questions over the strength of its vetting processes.

Speaking on Thursday, before the latest filming was broadcast, Farage told BBC Look East his party vetted "to a much higher standard than other parties" but "you can't vet for future comments".

Farage defends Reform's vetting after councillors filmed making racist comments Published 2 days ago

Reform councillor quits over offensive remarks Published 23 hours ago

Reform councillor calls TV report 'vote interference' Published 1 day ago

ITV News says one of its undercover reporters was asked if he would consider standing to be a councillor, after spending time leafleting with Reform activists.

He meets with the chairman of a local Reform branch in Chester, Ian Frost, who describes the meeting as "the first stage" of the vetting process.

After the reporter says he has previously posted in support of Robinson on social media, Frost advises him to delete the posts.

"Anything where you've got, things, Tommy Robinson or anything like that, okay, I would delete the account and I'd start again," Frost adds.

Farage has said Robinson would not be allowed to join Reform.

Frost later suggests the undercover reporter could apply to stand for the party, saying: "You might become a councillor. You might then want to go to the MP route. So, social media, yeah. And apply."

Frost told ITV News he thought the reporter was a genuine candidate and gave him the benefit of the doubt.

He added that it was not fair to judge people on a single conversation and he had since left Reform for unrelated reasons.

In another part of the film, a former Reform candidate - Alex Lomas - claims he failed the party's vetting process twice, including for sharing social media posts from Robinson.

However, Lomas says a few days after he failed for the second time he was asked to stand for the party.

"On my second application, I got declined on the Friday, I got an email from them on the Tuesday saying you've passed vetting," he is recorded as saying.

"I said, well, I think you better check with your paperwork, mate, because I've just failed on Friday. Now, you're saying I've passed it, I've not changed anything.

"And then I got a phone call a few days later. Hi, will you stand for Reform UK? I'm like, yeah okay."

He stood for Reform in local elections in Oldham in May but did not win a seat on the council.

The BBC has not been able to contact Lomas and he did not respond to requests for comment from ITV News.

Reform denies Lomas failed vetting in the first place.

Watch: Former Reform candidate claims he failed vetting process in ITV undercover recording

ITV's undercover report also shows Farage ruling a controversial mayoral candidate Dr Chris Parry – who said the then Deputy Prime Minister David Lammy should go home to the Caribbean – should be made to apologise, but not stand down.

In a conversation at Reform's headquarters, the party's director of communications Ed Sumner suggests Farage is "protecting" Parry.

In response Farage says: "It's showing a bit of sorrow."

In a separate conversation several weeks earlier, where Farage was not present, Sumner is recorded saying Parry is "clearly a racist" and "needs to go".

After apologising to Lammy in January, Parry was allowed to remain Reform's mayoral candidate in Hampshire and the Solent until he was later suspended in March "pending investigation" , following comments about a Jewish voluntary patrol service.

Parry told the BBC there was never an investigation and he has since left the party.

He said: "I would urge people to go back to the original contexts and tweets to see what was said and why. They related to reparations and failures by the police and government.

"They will see I always exercise my right to criticise anyone in power or the public eye, whom I judge to be acting against the interests of the British people."

In the report, Reform UK MP Sarah Pochin is filmed telling the undercover reporter that the party needed "women press officers".

"They are so chauvinistic... They just exclude you if you are a woman. There's a bit of a male issue going on."

Asked about her comments, Jenrick said Pochin was a "valued colleague" but added: "It is not my experience that the party has problems of that kind."

Labour Party chairwoman Bridget Phillipson said: "These latest shocking and deeply disturbing revelations go right to the top of Reform UK.

"Nigel Farage needs to wake up and realise the buck stops with him. He also must urgently explain why he allegedly stood by a blatant racist instead of kicking him out of his party.

"Time and again Farage has had every opportunity to demonstrate leadership and get Reform's house in order and every single time he has failed."

Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch said Reform "need to sort these issues out".

She added: "Every party will have people who make mistakes and have bad apples, the difference is how you deal with it."

stories.title: Councils warned of risks of high street pedestrianisation
stories.summary: The government says the process "needs to be well considered", warning that banning traffic could damage local economies.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
The pedestrianisation of Oxford Street in London has been subject to much discussion

Published 16 October 2026

The UK government has warned councils against ill-considered plans to pedestrianise high streets in England.

In evidence submitted to an inquiry by MPs, the Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government (MHCLG) said pedestrianisation can make high streets "more attractive, safe and welcoming".

But the department added that "the process needs to be well considered", warning that removing traffic could make high streets less accessible and damage local economies.

"Local leaders pursuing pedestrianisation must be aware of the risks and work to mitigate them, within a broader spatial strategy," the evidence says.

The evidence was submitted , external to the Housing, Communities and Local Government Committee, which is investigating the action needed to revitalise England's high streets.

An MHCLG spokesperson said the government had not issued formal guidance to local authorities on pedestrianisation.

The government is due to publish a new strategy on high streets later this year.

"We support local leaders to make their own choices about pedestrianisation based on the needs of their communities," the spokesperson said.

"Our upcoming high streets strategy will also set out more detail on how we are bringing high streets back to life and making sure they are accessible for everyone."

Studies suggest banning cars from high streets has become increasingly common in city and town centres across the UK.

Some councils attempted pedestrianisation experiments during the Covid pandemic, which spurred debates about the use of outdoor public spaces.

But the pedestrianisation of some high streets has proved contentious, particularly in London, London Mayor Sadiq Khan has clashed with the local council over plans to make Oxford Street traffic-free .

Parts of Oxford Street will be pedestrianised from 26 October.

The London mayor's spokesperson said he was focused on making high streets "cleaner, greener and more pleasant places to spend time, and helping to drive economic growth and prosperity".

"Pedestrianisation can help reduce conflict between vehicles and pedestrians, making high streets more attractive for visitors and shoppers," the mayor's spokesperson said.

They added the Greater London Authority would use data and feedback from the Oxford Street scheme to "understand how a range of people will use the newly pedestrianised space, and help refine the design of permanent improvements".

Most pedestrianisation schemes are immediately countered by some level of local opposition, said Professor Lee Ivett, who heads the School of Architecture at the University of the Built Environment.

He told the BBC that while opposition usually focuses on short-term disruption to local businesses, evidence does suggest that pedestrianisation increases the economic viability of high streets in the long run.

But he said pedestrianisation had to be paired with improvements in public transport to realise those economic benefits.

"If you want to defeat the argument that a reduction in the amount of traffic will reduce the amount of trade, then you need to also be able to make an argument that an investment in public transport infrastructure is actually going to be the vehicle that still keeps providing accessibility to the centre," Professor Ivett said.

In urban design guidance and previous high street strategies, the UK government has supported making high streets more attractive and people-friendly.

The last high street strategy - which was published in 2021 when the Conservatives were in power - said the government wanted to see more town and city centres "designed with a sense of place and to be attractive to people walking, cycling and using public transport".

But the government's approach to date has focused on giving local authorities the tools and flexibility to make their own decisions on pedestrianisation.

Pedestrianising roads can be a long and complicated legal process, involving consultations with residents and impact assessments.

It has taken a decade for London Mayor Sadiq Khan's proposal to pedestrianise parts of Oxford Street to come to fruition, after he first suggested it in 2016.

Elsewhere some pedestrianisation trials have failed. Last month, West Berkshire Council ended Newbury's evening pedestrianisation trial , after it was opposed by 75% of respondents to a public consultation.

In contrast, the majority of Stevenson Square in Manchester's Northern Quarter has transitioned into a permanent pedestrian-friendly space, following a successful trial.

stories.body:
Nearly 61% believe country is in recession and 65% of independents say economy is worse, according to new Harris poll

Tell us: what is your personal ‘recession indicator’?

With the midterm elections less than three weeks away, key voting groups including independents, rural voters and even some Republicans are increasingly disenchanted with Donald Trump’s economy, according to an exclusive Harris poll for the Guardian.

The majority of those surveyed were pessimistic about the economy, with three-quarters of Americans saying they are concerned about a recession while 61% wrongly believe that the US is already experiencing one. By its typical definition, the US is not currently experiencing a recession.

The poll shows growing weariness across the political spectrum over high prices.

Republicans, fighting to keep control of Congress, are losing support with independent voters, who are expected to be the deciding factor in key swing races. Nearly two-thirds (65%) of independents said the economy was worse, up from 48% who said the same in September 2024 in the heat of the 2024 presidential election.

Even within the Republican ranks, optimism has waned. In February 2025, just a few weeks after Trump was inaugurated, 39% of Republicans said the economy was getting better. By February 2026, just before the US launched attacks against Iran, that optimism was up to 49%. In the latest poll, just 28% of Republicans said the economy was getting better.

Voters say the high prices they are seeing at gas stations and grocery stores will be a key factor when they cast their votes in November. Two-thirds of those polled said that gas prices and grocery prices are their most important issues heading into the election, followed by living expenses, healthcare costs and foreign affairs.

Recent inflation data showed that annualized prices increased 3.7% in September, the highest reading before a midterm election, excluding the pandemic, since 1990.

Energy prices have been especially high since the Iran war, with average gas prices at the pump crossing $1.20 more per gallon compared with a year ago. California drivers, who are experiencing the highest gas prices, are paying on average $6.20 per gallon, according to AAA .

Democrats in swing races have spent much of the last few months framing their midterm battles as a fight, in part, against a growing affordability crisis. James Talarico, the Democratic candidate in a closely watched US Senate race in Texas, has a campaign ad of him holding a paper bag of groceries. “Too many Texans feel like they’re drowning, the cost of groceries, gas, healthcare,” he says in the video .

“They say I can’t win because of my name,” Abdul El-Sayed, another Democratic candidate for a US Senate race in Michigan, said at a recent campaign event. “My name is not the reason your gas prices are through the roof. My name is not the reason you can’t afford your groceries.”

In the new poll, a vast majority of Americans agreed that there was an affordability crisis, including 96% of Republicans. But Americans still remain divided over who has a solution.

Democrats (71%) were more likely than Republicans (59%) to say that their own party had a solution.

Republicans were more likely (26%) to say neither party had a solution compared with Democrats (17%)

Half of independents said neither party had a solution, while 14% sided with Democrats and 10% with Republicans.

Rural Americans, considered a core base for Trump, were more likely to believe that neither party has a solution (41%) compared with their suburban (35%) and urban (27%) counterparts. Four out of 10 of rural Americans said they were living in “survival mode”, where one surprise bill could sink them, compared with 35% of urban and 27% of suburban Americans.

When asked what is most affecting today’s gas prices, 46% of rural Americans said the US government compared with 28% of Republicans who said the same. Republicans were the least likely of any group to blame the US government, instead spreading the blame across oil companies, the Iranian government and natural economic fluctuations.

This survey was conducted online within the US by The Harris Poll from 24 September to 3 October 2026 among a nationally representative sample of 3,998 U S adults.

stories.body:
Voters’ opposition to the state of Trump’s economy is well established – despite his desperate attempts to deflect

Tell us: what is your personal ‘recession indicator’?

It’s indisputable that the political polarization of our time has reduced (and confused) the influence of economic conditions on US elections.

In September of 2024, in the waning weeks of the Joe Biden presidency, 65% of Republicans believed the US economy was getting worse. About six months later, as Donald Trump launched a trade war on the rest of the world with his “liberation day” tariffs, the share of Republican pessimists had dropped to 33%.

It’s hard to detect a reason for this in the economic data. Annual consumer price inflation fell from 2.4% to 2.3% between the two polls. The unemployment rate ticked up from 4.1% to 4.2%. Indeed, Democrats disagreed sharply with their Republican neighbors: from the last Harris poll of the Biden era to the first under Trump, the share who thought the US economy was worsening jumped from 28% to 73%.

As the midterm elections loom into focus, suggesting a stark Republican defeat, Trump and his minions are hoping that this ideological lens, shaping economic reality to fit political preferences, can prevent an electoral bloodbath in November. Maybe Trump can somehow dupe the Maga base into believing that “ we’re growing at a faster rate than we’ve ever grown before.”

From three weeks out, it seems pretty clear that the gambit is not going to work. Polling by Harris for the Guardian suggests that the economy is looking pretty bad even for their most loyal acolytes. Too bad to convince them otherwise.

The September reading of the consumer price index, which recorded a spike in annual inflation to 3.7%, had not yet been published when Harris performed its latest round of polling earlier this month. Still, the pollster reported that 38% of Republicans believe the economy is worsening. That is up from 29% a year ago.

The pattern is evident among cohorts that have proven historical Republican bulwarks. Rural Americans, loyal Republican allies for decades, are being battered by Trump’s policies. They were hit not only by his trade war, largely barred from China’s markets. They have been hammered by the rising price of diesel and fertilizer, for which they can thank Trump’s war in Iran. They have been hamstrung by Trump’s raids against the many immigrants in their labor force. And they feel roundly attacked by Trump’s attempt to tame rising beef prices by lowering tariffs on imported meat.

Unsurprisingly, this is showing up in the polling. Sixty-four per cent of rural Americans polled this month said the economy was getting worse, compared with only 52% of city dwellers. Six per cent more rural residents think the economy is worsening than in September 2024, during the last poll of the Biden administration. White Americans, another pillar of Republican support, are also turning sour: 61% believe the economy is getting worse, up from 48% in September of 2024. The share of men who believe the economy is getting worse increased from 46% to 52% over those two years.

Bill Clinton famously won the presidency in 1992 campaigning on: “It’s the economy, stupid.” For much of the 20th century the state of the economy was critical in deciding presidential and congressional elections. Voters blamed or rewarded incumbents for the state of the economy. The relationship was always moderated by partisan preferences, though. And it has weakened dramatically as the electorate has set on divergent ideological paths, ultimately splitting into rival camps with diametrically opposed perceptions of reality.

“The economic perceptions of Democrats and Republicans have polarized relative to Independents and that this polarization is not asymmetric in magnitude,” argued a recent study by political scientists from Stanford and New York University. They estimate the partisan gap in economic perceptions rose “from about 20 percentage-points at the beginning of the Bush II administration to a maximum of 73 percentage-points during the (first) Trump administration”.

after newsletter promotion

Partisanship doesn’t just affect voters’ perceptions of the economy. As reported by political scientists at Bucknell University and Texas A&M University, polarization reduces policymakers’ incentive to tailor policy to deliver broad economic prosperity.

“If voters are relatively unwilling to cross party lines to reward good economic performance or punish economic decline, then elected officials can pursue policies that distribute economic benefits narrowly without affecting their chances of re-election,” they wrote. “This might include aiming policy to deliver rewards to co-partisans, donors, or even to the office-holder himself or herself.”

This would explain Trump’s tactics to a T. Not only has he taken to scaring voters with culture war stuff – variously branding Democrats as apologists of Vladimir Lenin and claiming that they want to change the sex of young children. He seems to believe that he can sway the electorate by doing violence to groups that his Maga base dislikes, like immigrants and the “undeserving” poor. Maybe they will pay less attention to the cost of living, and to the Trump family’s self-dealing.

It seems too late, though. Voters’ opposition to Trump’s economic stewardship is too well established, having built up since the “liberation day” tariffs through countless destructive decisions over the last 21 months. He has not only lost average US voters – 58% of those think the economy is getting worse, 10 percentage points more than in the last poll of the Biden era. His shots at distracting the base are unlikely to convince them that they are not, in fact, miserable too.
