stories.body:
Low-interest loans kept many eateries afloat. But the industry never recovered enough for them to repay the debt

F or almost 20 years, Jai Mazumdar has served vegetarian curries, samosas, gulab jamun and other Indian delicacies at Spice N Curry, a cafe and grocery nestled inside a modest strip mall near Florida International University (FIU) in Miami. When the Covid-19 pandemic devastated his business, as it did with so many restaurants, Mazumdar took out a $370,000 economic injury disaster loan (EIDL) from the federal government in early 2021.

At the time, it provided a desperately needed lifeline. He was confident that once business returned to normal he could begin repaying the 30-year loan, which came with a low 3.75% interest rate and a 30-month deferment period. But when his business didn’t recover, the disaster loan turned out to be a disaster of its own.

The Spice N Curry cafe relied heavily on traffic from FIU. Since many students and faculty were studying and working remotely both during and after the pandemic, Mazumdar’s lunch business took a major hit. As the losses mounted, he applied for additional EIDL funds and was extended another $87,000 loan the following year.

Borrowers with EIDLs totaling more than $200,000 were required to personally guarantee the loan, which meant that if they default, the government would be able to seize their personal assets. Five years later, Mazumdar is struggling to make his monthly payments, and he’s losing faith that he’ll ever be able to fully repay the loans.

Since Congress passed the Coronavirus Aid, Relief, and Economic Security (Cares) Act in March 2020, the federal government has issued 3.9m Covid-related EIDLs totaling $378.4bn to businesses that faced hardship as a result of the pandemic. The Small Business Administration (SBA) was tasked with administering the loans – up to $2m per individual applicant. Despite the attractive rates and flexible terms, according to a congressional report released earlier this year, EIDL defaults have steadily risen to over 30%, resulting in $75.2bn in charged-off loans as of last June.

“Covid was an extinction event for tens of thousands of restaurants,” said Erika Polmar, executive director of the Independent Restaurant Coalition, a non-profit advocacy group for independent bars and restaurants in the US. “The ones that survived, if they didn’t receive [restaurant revitalization fund] grants, had to pay off all that debt from small businesses loans or EIDLs. Local initiatives that promised rent relief or eviction moratoriums often fell through. So they moved through 2022 and beyond trying to pay off their debt and weren’t able to reinvest in their businesses.”

Mazumdar says his business is worse off today than it was during Covid – a sentiment echoed by other operators whose businesses have been negatively affected by rising food, labor and energy costs. “There is a tsunami going on right now,” he said. “Rents are very high. The average population doesn’t have spending power. There is a lack of qualified labor. Tourism has also declined here. Everyone is just nervous about when the next leg of the stool is going to collapse.”

Five years after he took the loans, Mazumdar says the EIDL money is gone. Initially, he used the funds to refurbish the space and upgrade equipment, installing new refrigeration and freezer units to increase his retail inventory. He used the rest to cover operating expenses. After finally reopening the cafe in 2022, sales declined so badly that he decided to close the dining room permanently after just a year and a half.

“My monthly EIDL payment is $1,900, and my home mortgage is $1,600,” he said. “I had to rent out a room in my own home so I could have extra income to cover part of the payment.” His business has lost money every year since Covid, yet he’s managed to stay current with his loan payments. “I’ve been working seven days a week, 12 hours a day for the last three years. It’s become a completely hand-to-mouth existence.”

When borrowers exceed 120 days past due on their EIDL payments, the loans are transferred to the US treasury department for collection. That results in additional fees and penalties that typically amount to about 30% of the principal. When the loans are personally guaranteed, the IRS can garnish the delinquent borrower’s wages, tax refunds or a percentage of their social security benefits.

Randy Barnette, founder of the Virginia-based Ornery Beer Company, is almost two years past due on a $500,000 EIDL he took out in February 2021. Before Covid hit, he was actively searching for a space to open a second location of the Ornery Beer Company Public House, his restaurant and bar that features Ornery brand beers. The EIDL funds presented an opportunity to stabilize the business but also facilitate expansion; at the time, no bank or individual investor could have provided a six-figure loan at such a low interest rate, so he wasn’t dissuaded by the need to sign a personal guarantee. “I literally got an email from the SBA on a Monday, and a couple of signatures on DocuSign later, there was a half million dollars in our account in 48 hours,” Barnette said. “It was so easy, I was afraid I was falling for a scam.”

But when the expansion plans hit snafus, Barnette soon found himself underwater and struggling to keep up with his loan payments. After several costly real estate deals fell through, he was eventually able to open a second restaurant, which is still operating, but declining sales forced him to downsize the production brewery and shutter the original restaurant.

As the number of EIDL delinquencies rise among independent restaurant owners, some observers blame the SBA for relaxing the standards for creditworthiness too much post-Covid and approving loans to small businesses that were beyond their means to repay.

after newsletter promotion

“When you’re drowning in the ocean and that lifeboat comes by, you don’t count to see if it has enough oars, you just hop in,” said John Benson, a small business attorney in Doylestown, Pennsylvania, whose firm has seen a significant uptick in inquiries from restaurants struggling to manage EIDL debt. “These owners could not possibly have imagined inflation the way it is, tariffs coming into play or immigration affecting their labor force. The vast majority of them did the very best they could. They put the money into things that they thought would help the business.”

Despite the government’s aggressive collection tactics, which include recent SBA efforts to prosecute Covid-related EIDL and paycheck protection program fraud through Operation No Doze , Benson says his firm has had success working with the treasury department to reinstate loans that entered collection or settle his clients’ debts for lesser amounts.

For restaurants that are saddled with sizable EIDLs, the monthly installments are a significant drag on their business. “For what we’re paying per month, if you break it out over a year, it’s the cost of a high-level manager in our company,” said Dan Jacobs, chef and co-owner of DanDan and EsterEv in Milwaukee. His business pays close to $5,000 a month to service the loan he took out in 2021, which he said cuts his profit margin by one-third. “Meanwhile, we’ve seen close to a 15% drop in business from last year. And there’s no real reason for it, except the fact that the economy is trash.”

To provide extra relief for struggling borrowers, the SBA instituted a hardship accommodation plan in November 2022 that allowed businesses to reduce their monthly payments after the deferment period ended, but the program expired last March. “Once the hardship program ended, we stopped making payments altogether,” said Barnette. “Because we can’t. We’ve been struggling.” His loan was transferred to the treasury department for collection last summer. With compounded interest, penalties and fees, his total bill jumped from $530,000 to more than $750,000. “Maybe the smartest thing to do would’ve been to close down two years ago. Not one nickel that we paid after the grace period went to the principal.”

Bankruptcy law in the state of Virginia, where 56-year-old Barnette currently lives, has limited protections for homeowners. If he files for chapter 7 protection, the EIDL loan may be discharged, but the government can put a lien on his personal property; the state’s homestead exemption protects only $25,000 of home equity per individual from seizure. “My home that I’ve lived in for 20 years is the only thing I have of value,” he said. “I don’t have any life savings. I don’t have retirement funds. I’ve dumped everything into this business to make it keep working through the years. If I lose my house, I’ll just be living in a trailer park until I die.”

As a Florida resident, Mazumdar is protected from losing his home should he elect to declare bankruptcy. As of now, he intends to continue paying his monthly installments on time, even while his business continues to operate in the red.

With the midterm elections fast approaching, Barnette holds out hope that new leadership in Washington could provide relief for struggling borrowers. “Frankly, I’m just kicking the can down the road, trying to improve the health of the business, until Congress changes things,” he said. “We’re all holding our breath in the restaurant industry, hoping the political climate changes and maybe our leaders will do something about this.”

stories.body:
Exclusive: Isabella Weber prescribes a common-sense solution to poverty, inequality and fascism – making life’s essentials affordable for all

T he trouble with economists, Isabella Weber believes, is they do not behave like dentists. They obsess over ideological purity and are inflexible when searching for solutions, regardless of society’s symptoms. Dentists have no such pretensions – patients have little patience for dogma when in insufferable pain.

John Maynard Keynes, Weber clarifies in the canteen of the Wissenschaftskolleg zu Berlin (Berlin’s Institute for Advanced Study), was the first to draw this dental comparison – and she is running with it. As she sees it, the symptoms could not be more severe. “The status quo for the majority is entirely unbearable,” while extreme inequality and corporate concentration has reached levels “simply incompatible with democracy” worldwide. This is exacerbated by a climate crisis that “generates massive windfall profits” for big business as the “ecological foundations of our lives disintegrate”. All the while the far right is making hay.

This analysis echoes much mainstream liberal and left-leaning thinking. But Weber is concerned that her peers in the economic establishment act as if they are oblivious. “What’s common sense to most people is not to economists,” she says, and as such our economic system has “promised but not delivered”. She reels off disturbing statistics that highlight the growing disparities between haves and have nots. “As economists, we should do better. People’s dignity, and democracy, is at stake.”

In progressive circles, Weber, 38, is quickly becoming one of the most sought-after economists of her generation. An associate professor at the University of Massachusetts Amherst and an associate at Harvard’s Fairbank Center, she advises policymakers in the US, Europe and Latin America. She popularised the term “ greedflation ” to describe profiteering during recent cost of living crises. Her new book, Anti-Fascist Economics , is the culmination of years of research into inequality and inflation, and a lifelong commitment to fighting fascism. As she writes: “If we understand economics as the study of the material foundations of society, then economics is key to averting the catastrophes in front of us.”

Weber is calling on fellow economists to “abandon ideology” and develop a “big tent economic policy” that can counter an ascendant far right . Their gains, she argues, are not the result of a particularly compelling offer, but a direct consequence of traditional political parties refusing to acknowledge the endemic hardship facing their constituents, and the absence of a coherent economic vision from progressives, liberals and the centre right. “Currently, only the extreme right is willing to say yes, something is broken, and a different present and future is possible,” Weber says. “We can’t leave an alternative to this dystopia to them.”

In Anti-Fascist Economics , she pitches a solution: make life’s necessities affordable. That is housing, transport, food, water, energy, healthcare: the stuff humanity depends on. “Fascism is rising from frustration, born out of a crisis of livelihoods,” says Weber. “So, we need to reclaim these essentials now.”

Progressive politicians are already heeding her instructions. At a meeting of city mayors last month, the New York mayor, Zohran Mamdani, outlined how Weber’s work, which he had followed for years, had informed his affordability agenda in the city: free buses, universal childcare, rent caps, public groceries. Weber has consulted with other US politicians – Elizabeth Warren, Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez and Bernie Sanders – and UK ministers including Ed Miliband. The speech of the British prime minister, Andy Burnham, to Labour conference last month was Weberesque in its messaging. “Homes. Water. Energy. Transport. Care. Broken up and sold off,” he declared from the lectern . “Economic control diminished by selling off essentials.”

While it is a simple slogan, making the essentials affordable is a complex policy challenge. Each sector has unique properties, and functions differently from place to place. Weber argues that any and all levers should be pulled in pursuit of putting this floor under livelihoods, from novel approaches to centuries-old thinking. “The goal isn’t more state intervention,” she clarifies, “it’s just a tool, as are profits and markets to ensure affordability. In economics, we tend to have these overarching models and an inclination for silver bullets. I’m arguing not for universal solutions but nitty gritty detail.”

Take food, for example. At every stage of the value chain from source to table, she is urging governments to identify and implement interventions to keep prices down. At one end, four multinationals control between 70% and 90% of global grain trading (with profits that “thrive on volatility”). This does not optimise affordability. Her proposal? Create public buffer stock systems – publicly owned entities that can buy and sell grain into its market, not with the goal of maximising profits, but stabilising prices to protect producers and consumers. Keynes made this case a century ago.

A global public option would be a diplomatic nightmare, so Weber champions an orthodontist’s approach. She advised the South African government to pool regional buying power. “If the African Union developed its own buffer stock system, already this joint procurement would get them better terms.” Then, when prices are low, it could purchase; during peaks, it could sell to stabilise its market and provide regional insulation to shocks.

At the other end of the chain is retail. Weber cites the Mexican government’s canasta básica policy, through which retailers voluntarily cap the total price of a basket of two-dozen essential goods. In return, the government offers advantageous tariff rates and tax relief, “and at a weekly press conference lauds those who do a good job and calls out those who don’t”. In Mexico’s 2024 presidential election, the governing Morena party increased its vote share from 55% to 61%.

The environment sits at the core of Weber’s thinking: a policy that does not factor in climate is incompatible with her anti-fascist economics logic, she says. As Naomi Klein and Astra Taylor outline in their new book, End Times Fascism , powerful populists are embracing environmental destruction. “When these people say climate change is of no concern, they know it’s not true,” says Weber, “but they allow the planet to burn because they benefit from the fallout. If we don’t start acting effectively, significant parts of the global population will be sacrificed.”

In her book, Weber argues that fossil fuel dependency fans the flames of fascism: “Keeping essentials tethered to fossil fuels [leaves] ordinary people exposed to the price volatility of oil and gas that generates the economic insecurity on which authoritarian politics feeds.”

She is arguing for the stabilisation of a “basic allowance” of fossil fuels for individual consumption to ensure affordability, but warns that unless this happens alongside major public investment in green infrastructure, it is a zero-sum game. In 2022, publicly listed oil and gas companies raked in $916bn in global net income. “In research we conducted on the United States we showed 50% of those profits go to the top 1% of households. The bottom 50% of households only got a 1% share.”

“People can’t afford things, see the rich get rich, and become angry,” says Weber. If profits stream into shareholder pockets, Weber argues, inequality will continue to propel the far right. “There are dynamics and patterns in economics,” says Weber, “but how we shape and steer them is a political question.”

It is late August when we meet, just days before the Saxony-Anhalt state election in which Alternative für Deutschland (AFD) secured a milestone electoral victory . It is a “textbook example”, suggests Weber, of the far right’s success. Saxony-Anhalt is one of Germany’s poorest regions according to several metrics. “And with all its beautiful castles and villages,” says Weber, “it’s the perfect setting for the glorification of a mythical Germany of the past.” (This is one cornerstone of fascism, Weber suggests.)

The AFD’s campaign slogan in Saxony-Anhalt was “ alles ist möglich ” – everything is possible. As is often the case, the far right promises something better, while traditional parties of government offer stasis.

Weber has been sitting on the CDU-led German government’s commission on reforming fiscal rules . Tasked with looking at mechanisms to allow higher levels of borrowing to fund public investment, it should have concluded last autumn. “I can’t say too much while it’s ongoing,” she caveats, before adding: “We aren’t getting anywhere. Meanwhile our government is implementing severe social [security] reforms against the will of voters.” Witnessing the far right succeed, while her economist peers act as “a major blockage to economic policies that would rehabilitate faith in democracy? It’s made me desperate to hold my ground.”

Fascism is not an abstract concept to Weber. She was raised in Nuremberg, once a focal point of Third Reich propaganda. Family legend is that her grandfather, a priest in the Ruhr Valley, refused to hang a swastika in his church. As a small child, she realised “something so terrible happened that the only way to resolve it was to bomb our city to the ground”. During the 90s, resurgent neo-Nazis regularly marched through the medieval city. Weber and her grandmother would take to the streets in opposition. “I grew up with the threat of fascism,” she says, “and learnt that being anti-fascist and preventing its return is my first civic duty – in Germany, our democracy exists only because we defeated it.”

Weber is keen to point out there is precedent to much of her agenda, and not just the Covid-era policies that tore up the economic rulebook to safeguard livelihoods. Many post-war countries operated a “mixed economy with public ownership as a vital component … Neoliberalism has made us think this is the exception, but it wasn’t for decades.” Or look to Switzerland, which avoided privatisation in sectors such as telecommunications, water, energy and transport. While inflation across the OECD hit an average of 9.5% in 2022 , in Switzerland it only reached 2.8% .

What advice would she offer Burnham in Britain? “Renationalise water,” she says. “Invest in the NHS where people experience the state every day. Some form of rent controls. The proud history of council houses reimagined as models for affordable, climate-friendly living. The affordable food basket. Make public transportation very cheap, free even, in overcrowded cities.”

Much of this sounds common sense to a progressive 2026 audience, but even a few years ago, these ideas were on the fringes. In December 2021, Weber tentatively floated the idea in the Guardian that price controls could be used to stabilise the price of essentials. “It completely exploded with a hysterical reaction,” says Weber, “as if I was a physicist discounting the laws of gravity.” She became, as the New Yorker put it, “the most hated woman in economics”, mocked and ridiculed by her contemporaries. The Nobel laureate economist and New York Times columnist Paul Krugman said her argument was “truly stupid”, though he later apologised.

“It was a horrible time in my life,” Weber says. “But what I was saying is now being proved right. This experience has given me a calm confidence. These are intellectual battles worth the fight.”

At the New School in New York, Weber studied 20th-century socialism. “So much was utopian and up in the sky: nice ideas, but so removed from lived experience.” And so we return, again, to the economist-as-dentist: “In this movement, common sense must be the starting point to rehabilitate democracy.”

Anti-Fascist Economics: In Defence of Affordability, Dignity and Democracy by Isabella Weber is published by Allen Lane

stories.title: Porn showing choking or incest to be banned from early November, government says
stories.summary: The move follows a review into pornography regulation in 2025 by Conservative peer Baroness Gabby Bertin
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Published 16 October 2026

Online pornography depicting strangulation or incestuous relationships will be banned from early November, the government has announced.

From 6 November, it will be illegal to possess or publish porn which shows strangulation or suffocation, depicts sexual activity between people who are related or shows adults role-playing as children under 16 in England and Wales.

The new rules follow a review into porn regulation in 2025 which found depictions of choking were "rife" on popular porn sites and had helped normalise the act among young people.

Conservative peer Baroness Gabby Bertin, who headed the review, said the news came "not a moment too soon".

She told the Press Association the change in law would "send the unequivocal signal" to companies that host and facilitate porn, and also to wider society, that "extreme and violent content that encourages real-life harm is not acceptable".

Her independent review, commissioned by former Prime Minister Rishi Sunak's government, cited an account of a 14-year-old boy asking a teacher how to choke girls during sex .

It warned that people imitating such behaviour "may face devastating consequences".

Speaking to BBC Radio 4's Today programme on Friday, Baroness Bertin said porn showing strangulation had "absolutely sort of normalised this kind of sexual violence".

"That has to come to an end and I hope this law change will be the beginning of that," she said - adding that it aimed to "marry up" differences in the law about what was acceptable online and offline.

Non-fatal strangulation is already an offence if someone does not consent, but its depiction online is currently not illegal.

Amendments to the Crime and Policing Bill, which became law in April, sought to ensure such content would be captured by the legislation and made criminal offences in England and Wales.

Justice minister Alex Davies-Jones said it was not about "criminalising harmless sexual preferences".

But she said "porn can shape what people think a healthy relationship looks like, especially young people". Content which "normalises, or even glorifies" violence against women can "blur the line with what is acceptable in real life", she said.

"If you've got this material, delete it. If you're sharing it, stop," Davies-Jones added.

"It's not as harmless as you may think, and after 6 November, it is criminal."

'He strangled me without asking' - experts say choking during sex now normal for many Published 13 March 2025

The new offences each carry a maximum penalty of five years' imprisonment, for publication.

According to the government, this could include uploading, posting or otherwise making the content available to someone online.

Possession, meanwhile, could include keeping an image stored on a phone, computer or in cloud storage, the government says.

Someone found to be in possession of images depicting sexual activity involving a person pretending to be under 16 could face up to three years' imprisonment, after 6 November.

Those found to be in possession of images depicting strangulation, suffocation or penetrative sexual activity between certain relatives could face up to two years' imprisonment.

Porn that shows or depicts sex between step or foster-relations where one person is pretending to be under 18 will also be captured by the new offences.

Durham University law professor Clare McGlynn - who has previously warned widely available extreme content normalises sexual violence - welcomed the laws taking full effect.

"This is a potential turning point, the commencement of these laws marking a line in the sand when we decided that we were no longer going to accept the normalisation of sexually violent content in pornography," she told the BBC.

But she said questions remained over how swiftly tech platforms and regulators would act to remove and mitigate the spread of violating material.

"While these are criminal offences, this is not about prosecuting individuals, but transforming the online pornographic landscape and that requires the platforms and regulator to act," Prof McGlynn added.

stories.title: UK threatens to ban Eritreans over migrant return policy
stories.summary: The home secretary said she would not hesitate to impose measures on other countries "refusing to co-operate".
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Published 14 October 2026

Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood has threatened to ban all Eritreans from entering the UK if the east African country's government does not accept more returns of small boat migrants and foreign national offenders.

From Thursday, Eritrean diplomats will face restrictions on their movement outside London. Fast-track visas will also be stopped for VIPs.

Ministers have previously pressured other countries into accepting returns by threatening visa bans.

Eritrea branded the move a "perfunctory political gimmick", saying the UK had not issued a single visa to an Eritrean official since 2023, which the Home Office denies.

The country's embassy in London also accused the UK of refusing to engage in "meaningful and appropriate dialogue".

It said the UK had failed to disclose the return of criminals still serving prison terms and that the UK had claimed returns were voluntary "when clearly, they were not".

However, a Home office spokesperson said the Eritrean government's commentary "misrepresents the UK's position".

The UK had granted an exemption from immigration control for an Eritrean official in August 2026, according to the Home Office. Sources also said the UK hoped to restore co-operation between the two countries.

Human Rights Watch has accused Eritrea's government of widespread repression - including forced labour, conscription and restrictions on freedom of expression.

Eritreans were the most common nationality among small boats migrants in the 12 months to June - accounting for 18% of arrivals , external , according to figures from the House of Commons Library.

Mahmood said: "Eritrea has had every chance to accept the return of criminals and those with no right to be in the UK. Unlike other countries, it has refused."

She said she would not hesitate "to impose further measures on other countries refusing to co-operate".

The UK government accused the Eritrean authorities of "abruptly" withdrawing co-operation earlier this year.

The restrictions mean diplomats are banned from travelling 60km outside London without permission.

The Home Office said this mirrored restrictions on British officials in Eritrea's capital Asmara.

In the 12 months to June only seven people from Eritrea were returned there from the UK, according to Home Office figures. A further 244 Eritreans were returned to other countries.

Over the same period, more than 5,800 Eritreans arrived in the UK via small boats. A further 1,300 were given visas, mostly to join people already settled in the UK.

Dr Madeleine Sumption, director of the Migration Observatory at the University of Oxford, said targeting Eritrea would have little impact.

"Eritrea is one of the major countries of origin for asylum seekers coming to the UK - we had roughly 7,000 asylum applications in the last year of data, roughly 8% of the total," she told BBC Radio 4's Today programme.

"Most Eritreans who come and claim asylum are not removable at all - the government would never be in negotiations to remove them because 84% are successful at initial decision; more will be successful on appeal."

She added that about 1,400 people were initially refused asylum, but that this number would reduce after appeals.

Many young Eritreans try to leave the country - which is a one-party state - to avoid military conscription, which can last for decades.

Eritrea has never held an election since independence from Ethiopia in 1993 and there is no independent media. Critics of President Isaias Afwerki have been arrested and jailed for many years, often without trial.

Only four religions are permitted in the country – Orthodox Christianity, Sunni Islam, the Roman Catholic Church, and the Evangelical-Lutheran church of Eritrea – and followers of other religions have been locked up for years on end.

Last November, the Home Office said it was prepared to suspend visas from countries that "fail to co-operate with the return of their citizens".

Earlier this year, the UK threatened visa restrictions against Angola, Namibia and the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC).

Restrictions were announced against the DRC last year, but the Home Office said these have been lifted after co-operation on returns improved.

Angola and Namibia both agreed changes before restrictions were introduced.

But Sumption pointed out that the government may avoid targeting certain countries to avoid damaging trade relationships.

"If you're looking at overall numbers of people who are refused asylum and not returned to their country of origin, it would be places like Pakistan, also Bangladesh that are right at the top of the list," she said.

"But the collateral damage of a ban on visas for those countries when you have so many international students coming, for example, [and] a lot of people coming on work visas would be much greater than a country like Eritrea."

According to Home Office data, more than 20,400 people have arrived in the UK by small boats so far since the beginning of this year, down 40% from the same period last year.

There were more than 40,600 returns and deportations from the UK from July 2025 to June this year - an 8% increase on the same period last year.

Of those who had been returned, fewer than 6,000 have been convicted of a criminal offence.

The government requires people who are in the UK, but no longer have permission to live or work in the country, to leave.

This is called a return and can happen voluntarily or involuntarily.

People can lose the right to be in the UK for different reasons, such as a visa expiring, an asylum claim being refused, or by receiving a criminal conviction that results in deportation.

There were 40,605 returns from July 2025 to June 2026. This was up by 8% on the same period the previous year.

That number of returns is equivalent to about 6% of total emigration from the UK from January 2025 to December 2025.

Of all returns from July 2025 to June 2026:

5,962 had been convicted of a criminal offence 12,568 had lodged an asylum claim at some point 3,310 had arrived in the UK by small boat

People from India made up 27% of all returns from July 2025 to June 2026.

Up until September the UK was trialing a scheme with France to return people who arrived in the country on a small boat.

For every person the UK sent back to France, the UK accepted a number of asylum seekers.

This was called the "one in, one out" deal. As of 30 June 2026, 1,087 people were returned through this arrangement.

Returns can happen in different ways. "Enforced returns", which includes deportations, means the government arranges transport to return people to a different country. In some cases, people are escorted by officers.

All other returns are "voluntary". This means a person has agreed to leave and may receive government help with travel and other costs to help facilitate the return.

Some people classed as leaving the country voluntarily do so completely independently and without any government knowledge or involvement .

Independent returns made up 34% of the total from July 2025 to June 2026.

stories.title: It’s My Time review – Michelle Yeoh excels in Rocky-style quest to be Rubik’s Cube champ
stories.summary: True story about a former maths teacher who became a puzzle champion in retirement is squeezed into predictable sports-movie formula It’s not quite up there with Leonardo DiCaprio eating raw bison liver to get into character, but Michelle Yeoh reportedly spent two years learning the Rubik’s Cube to prepare for this Chinese drama in which she plays a real-life former maths teacher who became a champion in retirement. The true story is stretched and squeezed here, fictionalised to fit sports-movie formula; it ends up being so-so entertaining and funny in places, but disappointingly predictable. The biggest surprise is that cubing is so popular it has its own world championship. Still, Yeoh gives a superb, spiky performance as blunt, foul-tempered Zhao Yanhong; following a stroke, Zhao is living in a nursing home where she is the resident badass, assaulting her robot care companion and making illicit trips to the off-licence. She discovers her natural talent for the Rubik’s Cube when a washed-up ex-champion called Wu Youwei (Haoran Liu) comes to the nursing home to give a tutorial. What follows is a classic sports-film structure, with qualifying heats and Zhao training day and night, lifting weights and pounding the city streets. (Yes, running is de rigueur in a Rubik’s Cube movie; physical strength is Zhao’s weak spot says Wu, who agrees to be her coach.) Continue reading...

stories.title: Why Michael Gove worries about Britishness | Radical Thinking with Aditya Chakrabortty
stories.summary: For more than three decades, Michael Gove has been a leading figure in British Conservatism. As a journalist, government minister and now editor of the Tory bible, the Spectator, he has helped shape the right even as it has moved further rightwards. In the latest episode of Radical Thinking, Gove joins Aditya Chakrabortty to discuss the future of the right, his record on Brexit and austerity, and the Spectator’s position on Islam. Aditya’s suggested reading: To read the fruits of Michael Gove’s dalliance with the Marxism Today gang, look up his essay in a 1998 collection called The Moderniser’s Dilemma: Radical Politics in the Age of Blair. stories.title: We’re Asking the Wisconsin Supreme Court to End Warrantless ALPR Searches
stories.summary: Today, EFF joined the ACLU of Wisconsin in filing a petition to the Wisconsin Supreme Court, asking it to rule that the state’s constitution requires a warrant for retrospective searches of ALPR databases used by law enforcement in four cities: Milwaukee, Racine, Kenosha, and Green Bay. We represent a religious organization, the Wisconsin Council of Churches, as well as an individual pastor in Green Bay. As the petition explains: Right now, Automated License Plate Readers (“ALPRs”) are recording the movements of vast numbers of Wisconsin drivers as they seek medical care, attend 12-step recovery meetings, attend religious services, participate in protests, attend political meetings, and engage in many other private, sensitive activities. Law enforcement entities throughout Wisconsin collect, store, share, and aggregate this ALPR data. Then they search it, retrospectively tracking the movements of individuals and entire communities in ways that would have been prohibitively costly, if not outright impossible, before the advent of ALPR technology. We all deserve to be free of warrantless mass surveillance. We all deserve to live in a country where surveillance vendors cannot help police upend our system of individualized suspicion. Religious organizations and officials like our clients have a heightened interest in protecting their location privacy because of the range of expressive associations their work entails, including facilitating gatherings for religious worship, as well as offering pastoral care, confidential counseling, and community support. Likewise, the people who visit houses of worship have a strong right to privacy against police monitoring of when they pray, seek addiction counseling, or attend a domestic violence survivor meeting. This is our second lawsuit challenging warrantless ALPR searches, following SIREN v. San Jose. Earlier this month, a federal court in Oklahoma became the first to rule that ALPRs are a “type of indiscriminate mass surveillance” and suppress evidence from a warrantless ALPR search. We hope the Wisconsin Supreme Court will agree. Read the Wisconsin Supreme Court petition Read the press release Related Cases: Wisconsin Council of Churches v. Milwaukee, Racine, Kenosha & Green Bay
